code:
The **only** backend call in the entire frontend is `POST /users/profile` from `app/(app)/create-profile.tsx`. So profile creation is the one flow that needs the API running; everything else works with the backend stopped.

⚠️ **Those direct writes run with the anon key, so RLS is the only thing authorising them.** Nothing client-side stops a user inserting a `coach_athlete` row for someone else's athlete or updating another user's set.

**All backend calls go through `lib/api/client.ts`.** Do not hand-roll a `fetch`:

```ts
import { api, describeApiError } from "@/lib/api/client";

await api.post("/users/profile", payload);
```

It owns three things that were each a bug waiting to happen:

- **Base URL, with a named failure.** A missing `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` used to become the literal string `"undefined"` in the URL, which React Native reports as `Network request failed` — indistinguishable from a real connectivity problem. It now throws `ApiConfigError` naming the variable.
- **The auth header**, read from the live Supabase session (`getSession()`), so a caller cannot send a stale token. Pass `accessToken` to override.
- **The error envelope.** `ApiError.messages` is always an array, whether the server sent a string (thrown exception) or an array (`ValidationPipe`). The old inline fetch read `errorData.error` — a field the API has never sent — so every validation failure showed a generic fallback and discarded the per-field messages. `describeApiError(error, fallback)` gives you one string for an `Alert`, and handles non-JSON 502s, which matters once this sits behind an ALB.

## Conventions

- **Imports use the `@/*` alias** from `app/`, `components/` and `contexts/` — `@/*` maps to `./*` (project root, so `@/lib/...`). Siblings inside `components/ui` import each other relatively, so the barrel can't cycle through itself.
- **Types live in `types/`, split per resource** (`coach`, `conversation`, `reference`, `user`, `workout`) behind a barrel — import from `@/types`, never a specific file. They were one `types/types.ts`, which every migration slice would have had to edit, making a merge conflict guaranteed on each. `Profile` / `Federation` / `Division` / `WeightClass` moved here out of `create-profile.tsx`.
  - Watch nullability: reference-data `name` columns are nullable, and `id` columns are **uuid strings**, not numbers. The old local interfaces declared `Federation.id: number` and `WeightClass.sort_order: boolean`; both were wrong and typechecked only because Supabase's `data` is untyped.
- Double quotes. TS is `strict`, so no implicit `any`.
- Icons: `lucide-react-native` throughout. `@expo/vector-icons` is installed but no longer used in app code — don't reintroduce it.
- Fonts load in `app/_layout.tsx` via `useFonts` behind `SplashScreen.preventAutoHideAsync()`. **A new weight must be added both to that `useFonts` call and to `fontFamily` in `theme/tokens.js`** — a family name with no loaded face falls back to system silently.

1. `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` values are **inlined at bundle time**. Never put a secret behind that prefix, and restart Metro with `--clear` after editing — a running server won't pick up changes.
2. **`localhost` will not resolve from a physical device.** Use the machine's LAN IP. This is the most common cause of "Network request failed" on create-profile.

- **`WireEnumTest`** drives off the enum constants themselves, so a new value is covered the moment it is added: round-tripping, unique lowercase wire forms, case and whitespace tolerance, and empty (never an exception) for null, blank, unknown and injection-shaped input.
- **`EnumSchemaAlignmentTest`** reads the allowed values out of `pg_constraint` and compares them to the enum, then writes every value to the real table. ### binder_item

The tree structure — folders, documents, trash. This is the Scrivener "binder."

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

| type | enum | `folder` \| `document` \| `trash` |
| title | text | |

Manual or auto point-in-time captures of a document's content (Scrivener's snapshot feature).

escaped but their scheme was never checked, so a document containing

escaping. isSafeHref now allowlists http, https, mailto and relative

nobody has listed. An unsafe link loses its anchor, keeps its text, and warns.
Markdown gets the same treatment, since markdown links execute in renderers.

afterwards. Reading the mapping rather than a hand-written list means a new

GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67: prevent arbitrary certificate revocation via duplicate DB rows

Certificate identity was tracked only by Lemur's internal database row, not
by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could upload a
duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing
authority_id and serial) and then revoke it, causing the CA to revoke the
real certificate belonging to another user.

- POST /api/1/certificates/upload now requires AuthorityPermission on the
  specified authority, and rejects uploads whose (authority_id, serial)
  pair already matches an existing certificate (409).
- PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke now checks authorization and endpoint
  attachment against every certificate row sharing (authority_id, serial)
  with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request.

* feat(events): measure where events are appended, and audit provider areas

A `provider` is defined as the effect provider that APPENDS the event,
and a provider is a tool bound to an area of the tree. Nothing checked
that. The existing comparison reads the declared provider against the
declaring tool — one declaration against another — and never looks at
the append site.

That left two failures indistinguishable from health. A provider naming
the wrong area produced no diagnostic at all. And a reported
disagreement could be "repaired" by adopting the declaring tool, which
buys agreement while asserting an append site that does not exist: the
comparison agreeing with itself rather than with the tree.

The census parses the tree rather than reading a table, because a
declared append-site list drifts the moment an append moves, and drifts
silently — the only thing that could catch it is the measurement it
replaced. The parser is injected for the reason the evidence census
gives: only the compiler can be trusted about bindings, and `typescript`
is a devDependency that shipped `src/` may not import. An append whose
type does not reduce to a string is reported unresolved, never dropped,
since "could not read" and "does not emit" are opposite answers.

It finds 14 mismatches on the live tree, several of which no existing
check reports: `gate.executed` is appended from two areas at once, two
worktree events are appended from `workflow/compensation.ts` while
annotated to `verbs/`, and `review.routed` — whose stale-cover finding
was repaired one commit ago — is appended from an area no provider
governs. The stale-cover repair was correct and this is a different
fault on the same event, which is the point of measuring both.

The baseline lives in the test as a shrink-only ratchet, NOT as a
disposition table in `src/`. The audit keeps reporting all 14 on every
run; the test only pins today's shape so the set cannot grow …

feat(discovery): site discovery — a scan that cannot change your plant (#161)

* feat(discovery): scan types, industrial port allowlist, and safety profiles

The base of the site-discovery ladder — pure data and types, no sockets yet.

The allowlist is the safety argument in code: a fixed ~16-entry table with a
per-port rationale, a NEVER_SCAN table naming the damage each forbidden probe
would do, and NEVER_IDENTIFIED for protocols a sweep must never speak at all.
secsgem is the load-bearing case — a fab tool typically accepts ONE host
connection, so an HSMS session opened to 'identify' it can evict the real MES
host. Port 5000 stays scannable for MTConnect (HTTP is refused harmlessly by an
HSMS listener); the protocol does not.

Profiles bind stages + ports + pacing together so a cautious posture cannot be
half-applied. 'passive' emits nothing; 'legacy-safe' sweeps only, one host at a
time, for 1990s controllers where even a well-formed identify is a risk.

Found in review, not by a failing test: PacingPolicy's hard ceilings were
annotated Final, which still makes them dataclass FIELDS — a caller could pass
HARD_MAX_CPS=9999 and lift their own limit, defeating the one thing the class
promises. Now ClassVar, mutation-checked by a guard test.

* feat(discovery): pacing brakes, the wire log, and the no-write guard

Lands before any socket code, deliberately — these are what make the scan's
safety claim checkable rather than promised.

Pacing has four independent brakes because they fail differently: a global token
bucket, a concurrency cap, a per-host gate (one in-flight probe per host — rate
limiting alone still permits 20 connects/s all aimed at one fragile controller),
and segment health that drops a repeatedly-failing host and aborts a run whose
whole segment is failing, on the assumption that we are the cause. Host order is
a seeded shuffle: a march up the subnet concentrates every connect on one
switch's port group, which is what an IDS is tuned to notice.

WireLog only accepts a DECLARED packet class. A stage that starts emitting
something new has to add it to KNOWN_KINDS, next to every other thing this
product is willing to put on an OT network — so the report's counts, and its
'never done' list, stay true by construction rather than by memory.

The guard reads the package's own AST and fails if a write becomes reachable.
Two checks, because they catch different mistakes: an exact import check (which
is how the generically-named BAS write, , is caught without flagging
every local variable of that name) and an identifier scan for the unambiguous
ones. A sync test against the MCP write manifest means an 11th upstream write
tool fails the build instead of quietly falling outside the list.

Two bugs found while testing, both by the tests hanging rather than failing:
- TokenBucket compared refilled tokens with a strict >=, so a sleep of
  deficit/rate landed a few float ulps short and the loop span forever on
  ever-smaller sleeps. Now compared with a tolerance, mutation-checked.
- A hung limiter is a hung scanner, and on a plant floor a stuck process beats
  no error only in the worst sense. The refill loop now raises after a bounded
  number of rounds instead of spinning.

* feat(discovery): the dry-run preview — exhaustive, signable, zero emissions

The first thing anyone can run against a plant network is now the thing that
puts no packets on it. Given a plan, this derives the exact host list, the exact
ports with the identify call permitted on each, the worst-case duration under
the rate limits, and — as prominently as the rest — the list of what the scan
will never do. That page is what a controls engineer signs before the first
packet, and its whole value is that it needs nothing touched to produce.

Honesty properties, each pinned: the preview's declared per-stage packet classes
are checked to be real wire-log classes, so what it promises and what the report
later proves come from one vocabulary; a profile needing sign-off reports
authorized:false rather than looking ready; network and broadcast addresses are
dropped automatically, since a broadcast address is the one address a scan must
never connect to. 'Emits nothing' is proven by running it with every socket
entry point monkeypatched to raise, not asserted in a docstring.

Two refusals rather than best-effort: a prefix shorter than /16 is a mistyped
prefix until acknowledged on the plan, and 4096 hosts is the cap for one run.

Found while testing: the scope was expanded before the cap was checked, so a /8
materialised 16.7M address strings on the way to being rejected — 11s in the
suite, and an out-of-memory on an edge box. The cap is now decided by address
arithmetic (exclusions included, or a legitimately-narrowed large scope would be
refused); the same tests run in 0.05s.

* feat(discovery): L1 — the gentle TCP sweep

The first code here that puts a packet on a wire, and deliberately the least a
scanner can do while still learning something: one ordinary TCP connect per
allowlisted port, orderly shutdown, close. No payload, no raw socket, no
half-open SYN, no ICMP, no retry storm — a full handshake from the kernel's own
stack is what any client does, and the one thing a device cannot mistake for an
attack. Shutdown before close because some embedded stacks hold a connection
slot until they see the FIN.

The verdict is three-valued and the values never merge. 'refused' proves the
host is ALIVE and simply runs no industrial service — a positive finding, not an
absence — while 'filtered' means a silent drop, usually an ACL. A host-unreachable
errno is filtered too, not alive: a router answered on the host's behalf, so the
host itself said nothing. diagnose_empty_sweep() reports these separately because
they look identical in a summary and are completely different to act on, and a
silent empty list is never returned.

Tested in two layers: a scripted connector drives every verdict exactly
(including errnos a laptop cannot produce on demand), and a real socket listener
matrix proves the connect path against the kernel rather than against our idea of
it. A genuine 'filtered' needs a real DROP rule, so that one is left for the
Linux verification run rather than faked and called verified.

Found by measuring rather than reading: work was submitted host-major, so one
host's ports queued back to back, the host gate serialised them, and they held
the whole concurrency budget while blocked — 2.05s for a run that should take
0.62s, and worse on the deep profile's 13 ports. Two fixes: submit port-major so
consecutive probes are different hosts (also gentler per device than bursting six
ports at one), and take the host gate BEFORE the concurrency slot so a thread
waiting out a gap holds neither a slot nor a spent token. The preview's duration
estimate is what an operator agreed a maintenance window on, so it has to stay
true. Both pinned, the ordering one mutation-checked.

* feat(modbus): FC43 device identification — identify without touching a register

The scan needs to ask a Modbus slave 'what are you'. The obvious way, reading
holding register 0, is a data-plane request against an address the device may not
map, and legacy slaves answer an unmapped address by raising, dropping the
session, or faulting. FC43/MEI-14 asks the protocol layer instead, so nothing in
the process image is touched — proven by a test that makes every register read on
the connector explode and requires identification to still succeed.

Honest degradation is the point, not the happy path. Many simple slaves do not
implement FC43 and answer 'illegal function' — the device ANSWERED, so it is
alive and reachable, which is exactly what OTProtocolError means here and lets
the caller record 'identified by port only' instead of inventing a vendor. A
server that answers FC43 with an empty object set is identified as
Modbus-speaking and nothing more; the vendor field stays empty rather than
becoming 'Unknown'. more_follows is reported and never chased — continuations
cost extra packets and identification does not need them.

Verified against a real pymodbus server, not only a fake, and that is what caught
the actual bug: the decoder tried ASCII first, so 汇川 / 三菱電機 / Müller — entirely
ordinary vendor names in this market — were all flagged 'undecodable'. A
corruption warning on a good asset-register row teaches the reader to ignore the
flag. UTF-8 is now tried first and only genuinely non-UTF-8 bytes fall back to
latin-1 and get flagged, since latin-1 never raises and so can silently
mis-render. Every fake had used ASCII bytes, so the fake and the decoder agreed
and were both wrong; the non-ASCII vendor name in the LIVE fixture is what
exposed it.

Also recorded in the live fixture: pymodbus keeps device identity in
process-wide state, so a server started with identity=None still answers with a
previously-constructed identity. Checked in a clean process — identity=None
returns information={}, an empty answer rather than an exception.

* feat(opcua): identify a server via GetEndpoints, without opening a session

The scan needs to identify an OPC-UA server. server_info goes through
opcua_session and therefore takes one of the server's session slots — embedded
servers commonly allow only two to five, so an unattended re-scan can evict the
plant's real SCADA client from its own PLC. GetEndpoints runs on the secure
channel before any session exists, so it costs the server nothing it counts.
Pinned by probing eight times in a row against a real server and then requiring a
genuine session to still be available.

The security policies come back too, which makes this useful beyond naming the
device: 'still offers SecurityPolicy None with Anonymous tokens' is a finding an
IEC 62443 review acts on, and it is visible without authenticating. Reported as
plain booleans, flagged on the WEAKEST endpoint — an attacker picks that one, so
a mixed server must not average it away.

Verified against a real asyncua server, not only a fake, because the fake's
attribute names were mine to choose and that is exactly how a fake and its parser
agree while both being wrong. The real objects confirm each guess:
SecurityPolicyUri does carry the '#None' fragment, SecurityMode is an enum whose
value is an int, Server.ApplicationName is a LocalizedText needing .Text, and
UserIdentityTokens are UserTokenPolicy objects.

The teardown is load-bearing in a way worth spelling out: asyncua's sync Client
starts a NON-DAEMON ThreadLoop in its CONSTRUCTOR, so a probe that skips
disconnect leaks a thread every time and the process then never exits. Removing
that line does not turn the leak tests red — it HANGS the run, which is how the
mutation check proved it. Both the success and the failure path are covered; the
failure path is the one that bites, since a dead endpoint has the loop already
running by the time the connect fails.

* test(discovery): prove the filtered verdict against a real firewall rule

refused and filtered are the two findings this scanner refuses to merge — one
proves the host is ALIVE and simply runs no industrial service, the other usually
means an ACL between here and it, and they are completely different to act on.
Until now the timeout path was only ever driven by a stub raising TimeoutError
because the test told it to, which proves the branch is wired, not that the
kernel behaves that way.

This installs an actual iptables DROP inside a container's own network namespace
and probes that container's loopback: a real listener, a real refused port, and a
real silently-dropped one, all three verdicts asserted at once. Nothing outside
the container is contacted, and no host firewall is touched.

Verified on a Linux box with a container runtime — 9001 open in 0.01s, 9002
refused in 0.00s with alive=True, 9003 filtered after burning the full 2.00s
timeout with alive=False. Skips where Docker is absent, so a laptop still runs
the rest of the suite.

Also removes a comment in test_discovery_sweep.py that said this case was 'left
for the Linux verification run'. It no longer is, and a docstring promising work
that has since been done is the kind of stale claim this codebase keeps proving
costly.

* feat(discovery): L2 identification — one safe question per candidate protocol

L1 says a port is open. That is not an answer: TCP 502 open means "probably
Modbus", and an inventory built on "probably" is one a controls engineer throws
out on the first wrong row. This stage asks each device what it is, using the
cheapest question its protocol defines and never a data-plane read.

The table exists to route around four probes that would earn this product a
site ban. The diagnostic probes elsewhere in this repo were written for
endpoints an operator had already configured and consented to; pointed at
unknown hosts they are hazards:

  * Modbus — the obvious probe reads holding register 0, an address the slave
    may not map. Uses FC43/MEI-14 instead: a protocol-layer question that
    touches nothing in the process image.
  * OPC-UA — the obvious probe opens a SESSION, and embedded servers allow two
    to five. Uses GetEndpoints, which runs before any session exists.
  * SECS/GEM — never attempted at all. A fab tool typically accepts ONE host
    connection; taking it stops a production tool.
  * MQTT — a client-id collision disconnects the broker's real subscriber. Not
    part of automatic identification.

Two judgements are load-bearing and both are pinned by tests:

  * A rejection is a confirmation. A device answering FC43 with "illegal
    function" has spoken Modbus — it is CONFIRMED with an unknown identity.
    A transport failure is not, and leaves the port at port_only with NO
    vendor. Inverting these two produces an inventory full of invented rows.
  * A missing extra is a finding about this machine, not the device. Saying
    "could not identify" would blame a host that was never asked.

S7 is the only probe that sends twice: slot 1 then slot 2, because
S7-1200/1500 and S7-300/400 differ and one guess mis-reports half the installed
base. Both attempts are counted on the wire log, and an in-protocol refusal
stops the retry — the slot was right.

The preview's L2 emission list is now DERIVED from this table rather than
hand-written, so the document an operator signs cannot drift from the probes
that will run. The plan's invariants (no forbidden protocol, no undeclared
packet class, no protocol both probeable and not) are checked at import, so a
bad edit fails on load rather than in a plant.

56 tests. Four guarantees mutation-checked: the refusal/failure distinction,
open-ports-only, the S7 retry stop, and the identify gap. A fifth test caught a
real TypeError — host/port are TargetConfig FIELDS and collided with _target's
positional parameters, so four probes were dead against every live device while
every faked test stayed green; there is now a per-probe test that walks the
whole table and would catch it for probes added later.

* feat(discovery): L0 passive — read the kernel's ARP cache, emit nothing

The kernel already knows part of the answer. Every host this machine has
spoken to recently sits in the ARP/neighbour cache, and reading it costs
exactly zero packets — which is the entire content of the `passive` profile
and the only honest first move on a network nobody has authorised yet.

Three things decide whether "emits nothing" is actually true, and each is a
test rather than a comment:

  * `arp -n`, never `arp -a`. Without -n the BSD/macOS tool reverse-resolves
    every address it prints, putting a DNS query on the network per entry —
    which would make the one profile whose whole promise is silence emit
    something. Linux reads /proc/net/arp directly and the question is moot.
  * `(incomplete)` entries are dropped. An incomplete entry is an ARP request
    that went UNANSWERED — the exact opposite of evidence a host exists.
  * Broadcast and multicast are not devices. Every cache holds the subnet
    broadcast; listing it would put 192.168.60.255 in an inventory as though
    someone could go find it in a cabinet. One bit separates all three cases.

MAC addresses are normalized because two kernels print the same NIC
differently — Linux writes 48:21:0b:33:57:94, macOS writes 48:21:b:33:57:94.
Left alone, one device becomes two assets the moment a survey is run from a
different laptop. Verified against both real kernels: after normalization the
two machines agree exactly on the devices they share.

An unreadable cache produces a NOTE, never a silent empty table — "nothing is
on this network" and "I could not look" are different answers and only one of
them is about the network. Same for an unsupported platform.

24 unit tests over fixture text copied verbatim from both real kernels, plus a
docker-gated live test that sends a genuinely unanswered ARP inside a
container's own netns (an unused address on its docker bridge, so nothing on
the host network is contacted) and asserts the kernel's real incomplete row is
not reported as a device — with the complement asserted too, so a filter that
discarded everything could not pass by accident.

* feat(discovery): the scan runner — a plan in, an honest ScanResult out

Each stage was already careful on its own. What this level adds is the chance
to lose that, so the rules it enforces are all about the result never being
quieter than the run:

  * A stage the plan asked for that this build cannot run is NAMED in the
    notes. Silently running four stages when the operator authorised six is
    how a report comes to claim coverage it does not have.
  * An empty result is a verdict with a diagnosis. "No device answered",
    "every port was silently dropped", and "the hosts are right there and run
    nothing we speak" look identical in a summary and are acted on completely
    differently, so they stay apart — VERDICT_PARTIAL exists precisely for the
    third, which is the common answer on an IT segment.
  * The wire summary is taken from the log, so probes that FAILED are counted
    too. A trust page that tallied only successful requests would understate
    exactly the traffic an operator is worried about.

Authorization is enforced in the library rather than the CLI — checked before
a single packet, and asserted as such — so calling run_scan directly cannot
route around it.

Two fixes fell out of running it end to end for the first time:

  * A host dropped by the backoff now records that fact in its OWN row, not
    only in a run-level note. Its row has fewer ports than its neighbours',
    and without the per-host line that reads as an inconsistent scan rather
    than a careful one.
  * run_scan gained an identify_plan injection point. Without it the identify
    stage always reached the real network, which made the first smoke run
    emit genuine packets at a range it was only pretending to scan.

Hosts sort numerically (10.0.0.9 before 10.0.0.10) because a person reads this.

23 tests, including the one that matters most: the `passive` profile emits
literally zero packets even when a host in scope has an open port.

* feat(sink): on-box scan store — the tables the device inventory is read from

Sits beside the existing `samples` table in the same local database and never
touches it: a survey and a data collection are two products of the same box,
and one filling up must not corrupt the other.

Stores both shapes on purpose. The full result as JSON, so nothing observed is
lost to a schema that did not anticipate it — and flat columns (ip, mac,
vendor, model, serial, firmware, open_ports, confirmed) so the device table a
person reads is a SELECT rather than a program.

The judgement that needed a rule: where a host speaks two protocols, the flat
columns come from ONE of them and `identity_from` names which. A row that put
a Modbus vendor next to an OPC-UA model would describe a device that does not
exist, and a gateway speaking both is ordinary, not an anomaly. Both identities
survive in JSON regardless. Likewise an unconfirmed protocol supplies nothing:
port_only means nobody said what it is, so the columns stay blank rather than
borrowing a guess.

Saving is idempotent, keyed on a content-addressed id. A survey stored twice is
one survey — a store that appended would make the next comparison report change
that never happened, which is the most damaging thing a change-detection
product can do.

Nothing is pruned by default and there is no retention ceiling. `prune_scans`
is offered and never applied on its own: an on-box store that silently
discarded last month's survey is worse than one that grows, and it returns the
count so the decision stays visible. Keeping zero is refused outright.

25 tests. Four rules mutation-checked; one of them exposed a hollow test —
the port_only case had an EMPTY identity dict, so it would have passed even if
unconfirmed protocols were promoted, because there was nothing to promote. The
fixture now carries fields the store has to actively refuse.

* feat(discovery): the scan report — one self-contained file that opens with what it did

The section order is the argument. Most scanners open with findings; this one
opens with **what it touched**, because the reader of a first survey is usually
the person who has to defend having let it run. "We made 1,524 TCP connections
and 12 Modbus device-ID requests, and here is everything we never do" is
checkable against a packet capture. "The scan was safe" is not. The trust page
is section one and cannot be moved by configuration.

Two constraints are load-bearing:

  * Nothing is loaded from anywhere. No CDN, no web font, no remote image, no
    fetch, no stylesheet link. The file opens on an air-gapped laptop in a
    plant office and renders identically — a report that phoned home to render
    would contradict the product it documents.
  * Everything is escaped. A Modbus vendor field, an OPC-UA ApplicationName and
    an MTConnect device name are all free text chosen by the DEVICE, and a
    device on an unknown network is not a trusted source. Rendering any of them
    raw would turn a survey of a hostile segment into script execution on the
    surveyor's laptop.

A blank cell is rendered as a dash and marked as blank: the device did not
report that field, and it is never filled by inference. Where a host speaks two
protocols the table says which one supplied the row and leaves the rest to the
appendix, rather than describing a device that does not exist.

`host_to_dict` gives the runner's output the same shape the store returns, so a
report renders identically whether the scan came off disk or straight out of
the run — asserted key-for-key, because a renderer that quietly worked on only
one of them would go unnoticed until someone asked for a report of an unsaved
scan.

30 tests. Five properties mutation-checked, and one of them exposed a second
hollow test: "an absent field renders as a dash" searched the whole page, and
the HEADER renders a dash too — so it passed even with every table cell left
empty. It now asserts the marker only the cell renderer emits, plus the
complement, so a filter that marked everything blank could not pass either.

* test(discovery): the whole pipeline against a real Modbus device

Every other test drives one stage with the next one faked. This runs the actual
product end to end — a real pymodbus server answering a real FC43 identification
over a real socket, swept by the real sweeper, identified by the real probe,
written to real SQLite, rendered into the real HTML — and asserts that a vendor
name typed into the server's identity block comes out the far end in the report.

It needs a container for one reason: the allowlist permits 502 and nothing else,
and binding 502 needs root. That constraint is the product working as designed,
so the test bends rather than the allowlist.

Verified on the Linux box:
    VERDICT ok
    WIRE {'modbus_fc43': 1, 'tcp_connect': 6}
    HOST 127.0.0.1 [(102,'refused'),(502,'open'),(4840,'refused'),
                    (4843,'refused'),(5007,'refused'),(44818,'refused')]
    CANDIDATE modbus confirmed modbus_fc43 | vendor=汇川 Inovance,
              model=AM401-CPU1608TP, firmware=2.1.7

The vendor is deliberately non-ASCII. The one real decoding bug found in this
work was an ASCII-first identity decoder that flagged 汇川 as undecodable, and
it survived every test whose fixtures were ASCII, because the fake and the
parser agreed with each other and were both wrong.

Bringing it up exposed a misleading message in the product itself. The probe
reported "modbus extra not installed" when the module actually missing was
`cryptography` — a BASE dependency the connector reaches through the config
layer. That sends a field engineer to `pip install iaiops[modbus]`, which
changes nothing, on a plant floor where there may be no second visit. The
message now names the module that is actually missing and says whether it is a
driver or an incomplete install. Four tests pin it.

The scenario also prints its diagnostics BEFORE asserting: "partial" alone does
not distinguish a silent device from a probe that could not load, and those are
opposite diagnoses.

* fix(discovery): a sub-1/s rate must still grant a whole token

The token bucket sized its capacity to the refill rate, so any policy
below 1.0 connects/second saturated under the single token acquire()
asks for. PacingPolicy accepts anything in (0, 100] — and a rate that
gentle is exactly what a fragile controller deserves — so the gentlest
settings the ceiling allows would sleep out all 1000 refill rounds and
then raise, blaming the limiter for what was a sizing bug.

Capacity now floors at one whole token.

* fix(discovery): a hint narrows the port set, it never widens it

Passing any protocol or port hint flipped include_optional on, which
pulled in ports the chosen profile had deliberately left out. So
"scan only MTConnect" turned a six-port inventory sweep into one that
also connected to 80 and 8080 — ports the allowlist itself marks as
ambiguous with IT. Asking for less reached further, and reached at
ordinary web servers on the OT VLAN.

include_optional is now the profile's decision alone. When a hint
selects only opt-in ports the call is refused with the ports and their
notes, rather than resolving to an empty set and sweeping nothing while
reporting a sweep.

* fix(discovery): a hint that names nothing must say so

ports_for_protocols returns an empty set for a name it does not serve —
the right contract for a narrowing primitive, and pinned by its own
test. At plan level that silence was the whole failure: resolve_ports
handed back no ports, the runner's `and ports` guard skipped the sweep
without a note, and diagnose_empty_sweep then told the operator to
check their VLAN and CIDR while wire_summary showed not one packet had
been sent.

So a misspelling ("modbuss") and a protocol a TCP sweep structurally
cannot find (BACnet, FINS and HART are UDP) both came back as "your
network is wrong". resolve_ports now refuses either, names which it
was, and lists what is sweepable.

* fix(discovery): carry the abort as a flag, and cancel where it counts

Two problems in one path.

The verdict searched the notes for the word "aborting". That word lives
in a sentence in pacing.py, so rewording it — a change no test would
catch, since the tests assert behaviour and not prose — would have made
an aborted, possibly plant-disturbing scan report itself as ok. Any
future note containing the word would have flipped a healthy run the
other way. sweep_hosts now returns the abort as a third value and
_verdict takes it as an argument.

The cancel loop also sat outside the executor's context, so
shutdown(wait=True) had already drained every queued future by the time
it ran. No packets escaped — Pacer.probe re-checks segment health first
and _consecutive never resets, so each remaining future raised before
touching the network — but the code read like a brake that did nothing.
It now cancels inside the block, before the drain.

GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67: prevent arbitrary certificate revocation via duplicate DB rows

Certificate identity was tracked only by Lemur's internal database row, not
by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could upload a
duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing
authority_id and serial) and then revoke it, causing the CA to revoke the
real certificate belonging to another user.

- POST /api/1/certificates/upload now requires AuthorityPermission on the
  specified authority, and rejects uploads whose (authority_id, serial)
  pair already matches an existing certificate (409).
- PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke now checks authorization and endpoint
  attachment against every certificate row sharing (authority_id, serial)
  with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request.

    """
    The permissions system provides a way to assign permissions to specific
    users and groups of users.

    The permission system is used by the Django admin site, but may also be
    useful in your own code. The Django admin site uses permissions as follows:

        - The "add" permission limits the authUser's ability to view the "add" form
          and add an object.
        - The "change" permission limits a authUser's ability to view the change
          list, view the "change" form and change an object.
        - The "delete" permission limits the ability to delete an object.
        - The "view" permission limits the ability to view an object.

    Permissions are set globally per type of object, not per specific object
    instance. It is possible to say "Mary may change news stories," but it's
    not currently possible to say "Mary may change news stories, but only the
    ones she created herself" or "Mary may only change news stories that have a
    certain status or publication date."

    The permissions listed above are automatically created for each model.
    """

    name = models.CharField(_("name"), max_length=255)
    content_type = models.ForeignKey(

+
+## Normalizing the email address
+
+By default, NextAuth.js will normalize the email address. It treats values as case-insensitive (which is technically not compliant to the [RFC 2821 spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2821), but in practice this causes more problems than it solves, eg. when looking up users by e-mail from databases.) and also removes any secondary email address that was passed in as a comma-separated list. You can apply your own normalization via the `normalizeIdentifier` method on the `EmailProvider`. The following example shows the default behavior:
+```ts
+  EmailProvider({
+    // ...
+    normalizeIdentifier(identifier: string): string {
+      // Get the first two elements only,
+      // separated by `@` from user input.
+      let [local, domain] = identifier.toLowerCase().trim().split("@")
+      // The part before "@" can contain a ","
+      // but we remove it on the domain part
+      domain = domain.split(",")[0]
+      return `${local}@${domain}`
+
+      // You can also throw an error, which will redirect the user
+      // to the error page with error=EmailSignin in the URL
+      // if (identifier.split("@").length > 2) {
+      //   throw new Error("Only one email allowed")
+      // }
+    },
+  })
+```
+
+:::warning
+Always make sure this returns a single e-mail address, even if multiple ones were passed in.

fix(api): include component in exec authorization hierarchy (#4506)

Motivation:
When a role binding's scope is restricted to a specific component,
the bound role could not exec into that component, even though the
binding explicitly granted access to it. ExecHandler.ServeHTTP built
the authz.ResourceHierarchy for the component:exec permission check
with only Namespace and Project set, omitting Component, even though
the component name was already known at that point in the handler.

The Casbin policy matcher (resourceMatch in
internal/authz/casbin/helpers.go) only allows a policy path to match
a request path when the policy path is an exact match or a strict
prefix of it. Because the exec request's hierarchy path omitted the
component/<name> segment, a component-scoped policy's path (which
includes that segment) could never be a prefix of, or equal to, the
shorter request path, so it could never match and exec was denied.
Namespace- and project-scoped bindings were unaffected because their
shorter policy path remained a valid prefix of the request path.

Approach:
Set Component: componentName in the authz.ResourceHierarchy literal
built by ExecHandler.ServeHTTP, matching the convention already used
by every other component-scoped authorization check in the codebase
(e.g. service_authz.go, wirelogs.go). Updated the existing unit test
that previously encoded the buggy (missing-Component) hierarchy as
its expected value.

Validation:
Confirmed with a targeted unit test. Before the fix,
`go test ./internal/openchoreo-api/api/handlers/... -run TestExecHandler_AuthzEnvironmentContext_ExplicitEnv`
fails with a hierarchy mismatch (Component empty instead of
"greeter-service"); after the fix, it passes. Also ran
`go build ./...`, `go test ./internal/openchoreo-api/... ./internal/authz/...`
(all pass), and `make lint` (0 issues) locally. Did not run a live
cluster / e2e exec reproduction; the defect and fix are fully
provable at the unit-test level since the Casbin policy-path matcher
is exercised directly by the handler's authz check request, with no
live-cluster dependency.

Require authorization on certificates referenced via replaces/replacements

The replaces/replacements field on certificate create, upload, and edit
requests let an authenticated caller reference an arbitrary certificate
by ID without any ownership or role check, silencing its expiration
notifications and retargeting its rotation. Enforce the same
CertificatePermission check used for direct revoke/edit on every
certificate named in replaces before the request is processed.

Delegation is authorizable, the actor directory is consumed, and `dashboard` is part of the typed config.

- **`delegatesTo` accepts an object edge.** A synthesized `ask_<target>` tool goes through the same
  `RolesPolicy` gate as any other tool, and a bare-string edge carries neither `roles` nor `ability` —
  which is ADMIN-only under `DefaultToolAuthorizer` and an outright deny under `authzToolAuthorizer`,
  so delegation was unreachable under authz with no way to open it. `delegatesTo` now also takes
  `{ agent, roles?, ability? }` (`DelegateEdge`), whose annotation lands on the synthesized spec. Bare
  strings keep their existing fail-closed behaviour.
- **`ActorDirectory.resolveDisplay` is now called.** `actorDirectory` resolved into a provider field
  that was never read, so governance surfaces always rendered raw refs. Every governance route
  returning an `actorRef` now carries an optional `actorLabel`, filled from one batched directory
  lookup per page and omitted for unknown refs. Fail-soft: an unbound or throwing directory leaves the
  rows exactly as the read-model produced them.
- **`AgentConfig.dashboard` is typed.** The console's config block was read through an untyped
  `config.get('agent.dashboard')` string path, so writing it inside `defineConfig({ ... })` was an
  excess-property error. It is now a declared `AgentConfig` field and the provider reads it off the
  typed config.
- **`engines.node` is a range again.** Both packages published an exact version (`v22.23.2` /
  `v26.7.0`), which warns on install for every consumer on any other Node and hard-fails under
  `engine-strict`. Renovate's global `rangeStrategy: "pin"` had rewritten the ranges; `engines` is now
  excluded from pinning so it cannot happen again.
- JSDoc: the published source carried Portuguese doc comments (`sse.ts`, `spi/tool.ts`, `base-tool.ts`,
  `stores/factory.ts`, `rag/qdrant-store.ts`, `ai-tool-ref.ts`) — translated to English. Corrected the
  stale cost formula on `AgentGovernanceQueries` (it omitted the cache-token split), the attachment
  allow-list default (an exact-match list of 7 types, not `text/*`), and two NestJS-era references.

"author": "Davi Carvalho <davi@goflip.ai>",
  "packageManager": "pnpm@11.17.0",
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=20.6.0"
  },
  "scripts": {
    "build": "turbo run build",

model: () => aiSdkModel(openai('gpt-4o')),
  attachmentStaging: attachmentStores.memory(), // encodes bytes into a data: URL (tests/dev)
  attachmentMaxBytes: 20 * 1024 * 1024, // default 20 MiB
  // attachmentAllowedContentTypes: [...] // replaces the 7-entry default below
})
```

The route buffers the multipart `file` field, validates it against the size cap (`413` on overflow) and the content-type allow-list (`415` when disallowed), resolves the actor (the same fail-closed resolver as chat), stages it, and returns the `MessageAttachment`. The client then sends that reference on its next `chat` call.

### The content-type allow-list

The default is an **exact-match list of seven types** — what multimodal providers commonly accept as native image or file parts:

```ts
['image/png', 'image/jpeg', 'image/gif', 'image/webp', 'application/pdf', 'text/plain', 'text/csv']
```

There is no wildcard and no prefix rule: the uploaded type must be one of those strings. `text/markdown`, `image/svg+xml`, `image/heic`, and `application/json` are all `415`.

Setting `attachmentAllowedContentTypes` **replaces** the list rather than extending it, so spread

grading.service.ts khai kiểu `AuthUser` rồi đọc `currentUser.id` / `currentUser.roles`
→ luôn undefined lúc chạy. Hậu quả đã xác nhận trên DB dev:

- `getEffectivePermissions(undefined)` → `userRole.findMany({ where: { userId: undefined } })`
  — Prisma coi undefined là "không lọc" → trả MỌI user_role → hợp nhất quyền của mọi role
  ≈ super_admin. Mọi kiểm quyền trong certificates đều pass.
- `listMine` lọc `userId: undefined` → trả chứng chỉ của MỌI học viên.
- `POST /certificates/:id/revoke` và `GET /certificates/:id/pdf` (chỉ JwtAuthGuard, scope
  kiểm trong service) → user bất kỳ thu hồi / tải được chứng chỉ người khác.
- `GET /classes/:classId/my-gradebook` ném 500 PrismaClientValidationError.

Sửa:
- certificates + grading nhận `AuthPrincipal` và dùng `currentUser.userId`. Bỏ shortcut
  `currentUser.roles?.includes('admin')` — admin/super_admin nhận quyền ở phạm vi GLOBAL
  nên `hasPermission` đã phủ (đối chiếu seed: cả hai có certificate.*/grade.read).
- `RbacService.getEffectivePermissions` trả quyền RỖNG khi userId falsy, không chạm DB —
  phòng thủ chiều sâu để một chỗ gọi sai không bao giờ thành cấp quyền toàn hệ thống.
- Test hồi quy (+6): rbac userId rỗng (undefined/null/''), revoke 403 + tra đúng userId,
  listMine lọc đúng userId, getPdfBuffer IDOR 403.

Verify: `pnpm validate` 16/16, api 180 test. Live sau vá: my-gradebook 200; HV không sở hữu
`/certificates/mine` = 0 (chủ sở hữu = 1), `:id/pdf` 403, `:id/revoke` 403; GV vẫn đọc được
`/certificates/class/:id` và `/gradebook` (200).

Ghi nhận nợ MỚI (chưa vá, có từ P6/D1): sinh PDF chứng chỉ 500 với tiếng Việt —

fix: authorize before cancelling tasks in the chat delete endpoint (#27006)

DELETE /api/v1/chats/{id} called stop_item_tasks(id) before checking the
caller's chat.delete permission or ownership of the target chat. An
authenticated user who knew another user's chat id could therefore cancel that
chat's in-flight generation (streaming response, title or tag generation) even
though the deletion was then rejected. The chat id is discoverable through
legitimate read-only access to a shared chat or folder.

Reorder the handler to authorize first (admin, or owner holding chat.delete) and
only then cancel tasks and delete, matching the dedicated task-stop endpoint.
Legitimate deletions are unchanged; an unauthorized caller now returns 404 or 401
before any cancellation. The duplicated tag-cleanup and event-publish blocks are
merged.

## Phase 4 — Verify against the database (jdbc-platform tools)

Always follow this sequence — never skip a step:
`load_driver → connect → [tests] → get_test_report → disconnect`

1. **`load_driver`** if the driver isn't registered. Use CData short names (`saperp`,
   `salesforce`, `servicenow`, `googledrive`, …) — the server resolves the class automatically;
   otherwise pass `driver_class`. Verify `"status": "loaded"` and a non-null `driver_class`.
   If it fails, stop — there is nothing to test.

2. **`connect`** — **default to `read_only: true`** unless a test case explicitly requires a write
   path. Read-only is enforced in the JDBC proxy layer, so it covers **every** tool including
   `execute_java`: only `SELECT`/`WITH`/`EXPLAIN`/`DESCRIBE`/`SHOW` are permitted, and anything else
   is refused with SQLState `25006`. **`EXEC` and `CALL` are treated as writes** — a procedure body is
   opaque, and CData procs like `DownloadObjects` have side effects. So a read-only session cannot run
   stored procedures: if the ticket needs one, connect with `read_only: false` and say so in chat.
   It is a guard against an accidental write, not a sandbox — snippet code can still reach the
   underlying connection via `getMetaData().getConnection()` or `unwrap()`.
   Only set `trust_all_certs` / `set_jvm_proxy` when the engineer asks.
   Reuse the returned `session_id` for every later call.

   **Proxy:** Just call `connect` normally with the user's connection string **exactly as given —

- `get_test_report` — Markdown summary (pass/fail per criterion + session stats).
- `export_results` — write evidence rows to CSV when an attachment is wanted.

| `record_check` | Record a non-SQL pass/fail check | `session_id`, `criterion`, `passed`, `detail`, `sql` |
| `export_results` | Export a SELECT to CSV (UTF-8, RFC4180) | `session_id`, `sql`, `file_path`, `max_rows` |
| `get_test_report` | Markdown pass/fail report | `session_id` |

class HTTPAuthorizationCredentials(BaseModel):
    """
    The HTTP authorization credentials in the result of using `HTTPBearer` or
    `HTTPDigest` in a dependency.

    The HTTP authorization header value is split by the first space.

    The first part is the `scheme`, the second part is the `credentials`.

    For example, in an HTTP Bearer token scheme, the client will send a header
    like:

    ```
    Authorization: Bearer deadbeef12346
    ```

    In this case:

    * `scheme` will have the value `"Bearer"`
    * `credentials` will have the value `"deadbeef12346"`
    """

    scheme: Annotated[
        str,
        Doc(
            """
            The HTTP authorization scheme extracted from the header value.
            """
        ),
    ]
    credentials: Annotated[
        str,
        Doc(
            """
            The HTTP authorization credentials extracted from the header value.
            """
        ),
    ]

explanation:
Fix real vulnerabilities found in a dedicated security audit

Three parallel audits (auth/authz, injection/input-handling, secrets/
infrastructure) covering the whole app, adversarial lens. Fixes:

CRITICAL
- MFA was completely bypassable: the 5-minute "mfa_pending" challenge
  token issued by /auth/login (before a TOTP/backup code is ever
  checked) decoded and passed get_current_user()'s checks exactly like
  a real session token -- anyone with just a password (the one thing
  MFA exists to add a second factor against) could call any
  authenticated endpoint directly with it, no code required, for the
  full 5-minute window. Now explicitly rejected, same pattern as the
  existing "purpose" claim check.

HIGH
- Twilio webhook signature verification failed OPEN (skipped, request
  allowed through) when TWILIO_TOKEN/PUBLIC_BASE_URL were unset --
  now fails closed (503), matching the pattern already used correctly
  for CRON_SECRET/EMAIL_WORKER_SECRET.
- SECRET_KEY/JWT_SECRET ship with hardcoded, publicly-known placeholder
  defaults with no code-level guard against running with them in
  production (only Render's generateValue: true prevented this on the
  documented deploy path). App now refuses to boot with DEBUG=false if
  either is still its literal default.

MODERATE
- Three IDOR gaps: POST /communications/send's maintenance_update
  template, POST /maintenance/'s unit_id/tenant_id, and POST
  /accounting/expenses' vendor_id all accepted a foreign org's UUID
  with no ownership check, leaking that resource's name/title/status
  back in the response. All now validated against the caller's org.
- Unescaped HTML injection in three outreach-email templates
  (services/lead_service.py) -- lead fields (scraped from public,
  attacker-editable Google Business Profile data, or typed into
  POST /leads with no sanitization) were interpolated into HTML emails
  with no output encoding. Now html.escape()'d for the HTML body
  specifically (plain-text body unaffected).
- SSRF in the lead-scraper's email-discovery fetch
  (workers/tasks/lead_scraping.py) -- a Places listing's self-reported
  website URL was fetched with no scheme/private-IP allowlist and
  followed redirects blindly, so a listing pointed at an internal
  address or a cloud metadata endpoint would have the server fetch it.
  Added an SSRF guard checked on the initial URL and re-checked on
  every redirect hop.
- FastAPI backend sent no security headers at all (X-Frame-Options,
  X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) --
  only the Next.js frontend did, despite security.tsx's copy claiming
  this applies to "every response." Left /docs and /redoc unprotected
  against framing. Added a headers middleware.
- ALLOWED_ORIGINS="*" combined with allow_credentials=True (a plausible
  operator typo in Render's env vars) would silently make CORS reflect
  any origin with credentials -- app now refuses to boot with that
  combination instead.
- Three endpoints doing real, billed AI/scraping work (inspection photo
  AI analysis, the Claude marketing-copy generator, the lead-scrape
  trigger) had zero rate limiting or cost cap beyond role/plan gating --
  a compromised privileged account or a buggy retry loop had no
  built-in ceiling on Anthropic/OpenAI/Google Places billing, and on
  this single-worker server a burst could also stall every other
  tenant's requests. Added reasonable per-minute limits to all three.

Not fixed here, flagged for a follow-up decision (both require either
a schema migration or a product/UX tradeoff, not a mechanical fix):
- Password reset tokens (staff-side /auth/reset-password) are replayable
  within their 30-minute window -- not marked single-use like the
  tenant-portal equivalent already is.
- Rate limiting on login/reset/2FA is per-IP only, no per-account
  lockout/backoff -- a distributed credential-stuffing attempt across
  many source IPs isn't meaningfully throttled today.
- API keys are stored and compared in plaintext (high-entropy,
  infeasible to brute-force, but a DB-level compromise would expose
  live keys directly rather than hashes) -- hashing at rest would need
  a rotation flow since existing keys can't be un-hashed.

fix(reprice): P1 — split !userId (401) from ownership check (403) on POST /:requestId/reprice (#1913)

## Broken leg
The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Not authorized to reprice this booking' });
    }

Unauth callers ate a wasted bookingRequests SELECT before hitting a
MISLEADING 403 that suggested a permissions problem, not a
credentials problem. The audit agent classified this as "risky-cosmetic"
because it's a 403→401 client-behavior change; on inspection the reprice
client is always an authenticated logged-in customer, so a 401 only fires
for callers that shouldn't be reaching the endpoint at all.

## Fix (server-only, split into two clean checks)
1. Explicit 401 at the door — before the DB fetch — with an honest
   'Authentication required' message.
2. Ownership check no longer needs the !userId branch — reads cleanly
   as "owner OR verified admin".

Both branches unchanged behaviorally for legitimate callers.

## Test
server/tests/reprice-401-hygiene.regression.test.ts — 3 pins:
  ✓ returns 401 explicitly when there is no userId
  ✓ 401 guard sits BEFORE the first db.select() (no wasted round-trip)
  ✓ ownership check no longer folds !userId into the 403 branch

    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  3 passed (3)

## Dependency
None. Completes the auth-slippage sweep on booking-requests.ts —
prior sweep PRs #1904 (confirm), #1911 (7 POSTs), #1912 (GET). This
covers the last remaining router-mounted handler with the same shape.

## Risk
Very low. 401 replaces 403 for anon callers only (a case that already
denied). Legitimate customer + admin repricing unchanged.

Per standing CEO directive.

[T004] Mass bake: 840 tiles, 43 honest stops, and the recipe merge the census demanded (#121)

* [T004] Recipe v4 and its pre-registration, before a single v4 pixel is rendered

v4 is v3's colour aggregate over v2's packing. The mass bake needs it: the
Stage A census measured v1/v3 packing at 172 of 883 ledger cells unpackable at
ANY scale and a median applied resolution scale of 0.5, so baking the island on
v3's packing would refuse a fifth of it for a reason v2 already solved.

v4 IS A RECIPE CHANGE, so it goes through the discipline T013's gate adoption
made a condition of using A3'': predictions and bars committed BEFORE the
confirming capture, and a stop on a miss. A3'' = 0.035 is a post-hoc bar derived
from v3's own worst pose and cannot certify a new recipe by itself.

THE PREDICTION BASIS IS NOW PINNED, NOT ASSERTED. A flat face's colour is
computed once and written to every texel of its rect, so a 1x1 rect must carry
the same byte a 4x4 rect carried. far-tier-bake.test.ts pins the rect SIZES,
which is a different statement — a size test passes just as happily if the
colour is recomputed differently at a different size. The new test pins the
BYTES, and the pre-registration cites it.

What does change is the atlas layout and the global scale: on the prototype cell
appliedScale 0.5 to 0.7071 and delivered texel ratio 0.5 to 0.7071, so a
minifying filter averages a different neighbourhood. That is the prediction
under test, at |delta| <= 0.01.

ADDITIVITY IS ENFORCED AGAINST THE CELL'S OWN RECOMPUTED DIGEST, not against
T013's constant: v4 with facade-only colour and v1 packing reproduces the cell's
v1 atlas, and the recomputation independently lands on c159e050. That form of
the gate keeps working for every cell the campaign later bakes.

Byte replay PASS in-process and in a fresh child. GLB fc534a41, atlas f93873cc,
recipe fd950a77. v1, v2 and v3 keep their ids, hashes and frozen artifacts.

The cell bake is a MODULE, not a third copy in a third CLI: the cycle that
adopts v4 and the campaign that ships it must bake identically, and now they
call the same function. Every refusal it can produce is a named FarTierCellStop
rather than a crash — an unexpected exception is deliberately NOT converted into
a stop, because a bug must not be indistinguishable from a refusal.

* [T004] Campaign infrastructure, with its thresholds fixed before the first cell bakes

THE ZONE-FALLBACK BAR IS DERIVED, NOT PICKED. A wall zone with no attributed
surface keeps v1's colour while the tile says v4; T013 measured that at 0.059
per cent of wall area on one cell and left the share at scale unmeasured.

  share x 0.048 x 0.21 <= 0.001

0.048 is the relative energy the wall correction reaches where walls are visible
(4.81 / 4.73 / 4.62 per cent). 0.21 is the wall term's median share of the
chromaticity gap. 0.001 is the pinned instrument's own cross-session tolerance —
so the bar asks that reverting a zone stay under the noise floor of the
instrument that would have to see it. That gives 9.92 per cent; the bar is
HALVED to 5 per cent, because all three factors come from ONE cell and the
campaign is 883.

Under the bar a cell is ACCEPTED BY NAME with its zones and share recorded; over
it, an honest stop. Neither is silent: bakeFarTierCell refuses a fallback
outright unless BOTH an explicit opt-in and a bar are supplied.

SIX REFUSAL CLASSES NAMED IN ADVANCE, each with its expectation. packing-
infeasible is PREDICTED ZERO — the 172 unpackable cells were measured under v1/v3
packing and v4 is the fix for exactly them, so a non-zero count is a finding.
over-b2 CANNOT FIRE: farTierResolution clamps the atlas to 256 and B2 was derived
at 256, so it is a structural invariant asserted once against the constants
rather than a per-cell check that would be asserting min(x,256) <= 256.

NOTHING IS HAND-RECONSTRUCTED. Wave profiles come from WAVE_BASE_PROFILES, the
registry eight other wave CLIs already import; -c2 ids are COMPOSED through
exteriorTwoLodRetentionReleaseId over the typed EXTERIOR_SERVING_WAVES. The
tests assert IDENTITY — the profile must BE the imported constant, not merely
look like it — and the CLI cross-checks each committed package's own waveId and
cell count against the ledger before baking anything.

THE ORDERING IS STRUCTURAL. `bake` cannot write an inventory and `seal` cannot
bake; `seal` writes one only after every baked cell reproduces byte-identically
in batched fresh child processes. "No wave inventory before that wave's replay"
stops being a rule to remember.

AND THE STOP RULE SAYS WHAT IT ACTUALLY PROTECTS: operator time and record
integrity. It protects NO serving surface, because there is none — the far tier
serves one staged cell from the T003 root and this campaign writes to a
different, gitignored root that nothing reads.

Snapshot and ledger hoisted out of the per-cell loop (1.0 s and 30 ms once,
against 883 times); the per-wave -c2 inventory loads once per wave. What is NOT
shortcut is the fail-closed sourcing: every cell still regenerates its shipped
lod_0 bytes and verifies each against the committed package before a single
far-tier face is built.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [T004] Closure tooling: coverage arithmetic, the sample's sources, and the eviction obligation

Three additions, none of which touches a serving surface.

`summary` closes the coverage arithmetic MACHINE-CHECKED against the ledger and
refuses to write a record if it does not close: every declared cell must have
either a validated tile in its wave's sealed inventory or a named honest stop.
It also refuses if a wave has telemetry but no sealed inventory, so a summary
cannot describe a campaign that has not replayed.

It carries the DEFERRED EVICTION OBLIGATION with its arithmetic rather than a
sentence. FAR_TIER_RUNTIME_BUDGETS says evictionPolicy NONE and, in its own
words, defers the question to mass-bake scale — this task. The record computes
which of the two ceilings binds first at the campaign's real mean tile size, and
says plainly that the consequence is routine `over-budget` refusals at island
scale rather than the exceptional ones a single staged cell produced. It is
NAMED, not fixed: serving is T005's.

`emit-sources` exists because the shipped `sources` path carries a wave table of
two — w00 and w05 — and the characterization samples all six. It reuses the same
materialization and the same -c2 verification, so the subjects are the verified
shipped bytes; only the wiring is the campaign's. Smoke-tested on a w01 cell at
77 assets.

The characterization CLI pre-registers a DESCRIPTIVE population prediction:
A3'' plus an allowance of 0.004, derived as the WIDTH of T013's geometric-term
bracket (0.027301 to 0.030863) — the size of the one quantity that measurement
could not pin down, and therefore the honest scale for how far another cell's
geometry may sit from the prototype's. It is a prediction about a SAMPLE and not
a bar: a cell-level miss is recorded at stratum level with analysis, because
letting a six-cell draw stop a wave would be acceptance by the back door on a
sample never designed to bear it.

* [T004] The additivity gate was refusing cells the adopted recipe packs fine

Caught by reading the campaign's own refusal messages rather than its counts.
w01 recorded 22 cells as `packing-infeasible` — a class the pre-registration
predicted ZERO of under v4 — and the message said "each face costs at least 64
texels, so this atlas holds at most 1024". Those are v1's numbers. v4 costs 9
texels a face and holds 7,281.

THE CAUSE. The per-cell additivity gate bakes a v1 REFERENCE first, and I let
its refusal propagate as the cell's refusal. Midtown has cells of 1,031 to 1,853
faces: v4 packs them comfortably, v1 cannot pack them at all, and so 22 real
cells were recorded as infeasible under a recipe that handles them. The tiles
were never wrong. They were never built.

THE FIX. `farTierAdditivityGate` is now one function used by the campaign, and
it distinguishes the two cases: where v1 CAN pack, the gate runs and a mismatch
still fails the cell; where v1 CANNOT, the gate reports NOT-APPLICABLE with its
reason and the cell bakes. Every other refusal from the reference bake still
propagates — the tolerance is exactly one stop code and no wider.

Telemetry now records the gate's verdict per cell, so "checked" and "could not
be checked" are countable rather than conflated.

Tests pin the arithmetic the bug hid: v1's per-face cost is 64 texels and v4's
is 9; a 256px atlas holds 1,024 faces under v1 and 7,281 under v4; and a
1,400-face cell refuses under v1 while packing under v4.

The pre-registration is NOT amended. Its prediction of zero `packing-infeasible`
cells was a prediction about v4 and remains correct; what failed was my gate.
The stale w00 and w01 records are deleted rather than kept, because a campaign
record produced by a path that refused real cells describes nothing anyone
should read.

v1's 1,024 capacity and under v4's 7,281. Four real tests: PASS returns the
cell's own v1 digest; NOT-APPLICABLE returns applicable false, verdict
"not-applicable", a null digest and a non-null reason, without throwing; a
non-packing-infeasible refusal from the v1 reference still PROPAGATES, so the

something that cannot fail means nothing. The describe block no longer promises
what it does not test.

It now makes the module throw and reads the code off the error.

transcription with nothing between the instrument and the record the ADOPTION
rests on — the characterization path already did this right. The harness now
writes v4-measurements.json, the verdict reads it and records its digest, and

PASS; the verdict now RUNS the replay and records its result. Both re-emissions
carry the prior hash.

any of its zones reverted, and a face carries base and shaft independently — so
the 5 per cent bar is conservative rather than flattering. Stated in the
telemetry field docs, the campaign summary, and the pre-registration through an
amend path that ASSERTS the bar is unchanged and refuses otherwise.

the one root-level auth:sanctum route — still accepted agent bearers, giving an
agent a human-only action and a token-validity oracle. The refusal now sits on

surface will opt into (#135). The IDOR sweep enumerates every registered route
instead of a prefix, and proves its two exemptions authenticate nothing.

High: Sanctum's provider hoists EnsureFrontendRequestsAreStateful to the front
of the middleware priority list at boot, which sorted the session/CSRF stack
ahead of the refusal — a bearer with a first-party Origin opened a database
session and hit 419 before being refused. AppServiceProvider now hoists the
refusal after Sanctum's provider; asserted on pipeline order and as zero
queries on a rejected request. Mint and its audit record are one transaction;
revoke records through recordSafely and only the request that removed the row
records an event; the Policy trait fails closed on any persistent token that is
not an AgentToken.

`adr-2026-08-13` chose versioned typed finding identities (rubric + concernKind + anchor
references, hashed) but deliberately left each rubric's reference schema to be "carefully
designed." In practice that design happened incrementally in BUILD: successive
`build_review` laps of feature #1611 found each not-yet-canonical anchor field, and the
remediation planner authored a new reference grammar per lap — plan-task id grammar,
tautology test selectors (`rem-rootcause-7`), and finally a line-coordinate rootCause
hunk locus `path@oldStart,oldCount:newStart,newCount` (`rem-rootcause-9/10`, commit
`d8fa79150`) — 21 appended tasks against an 18-task plan, with no operator checkpoint
(intake #1695). The operator rejected and reverted the line-coordinate locus.

Forces:

- **Identity must survive wording drift** (the #1611 defect) — references, never prose.
- **Identity must survive rebases.** The sibling feature
  `rubric-cache-identity-is-sha-anchored-so-a-rebase-` (plan 2026-08-15) already ruled
  the same way for the rubric cache: content-only identity, because SHA- and
  coordinate-anchored identity breaks on every rebase that leaves content unchanged.
  Line-coordinate loci re-import exactly that fragility into finding identity: a clean
  rebase renumbers hunks, drifting every open finding's id and detaching accepted
  dispositions — recreating #1611 through the mechanism built to fix it.
- **The schema must be closed class-level.** A field-by-field schema invites the
  observed failure: each unspecified field becomes a future finding and an unapproved
  grammar. The vocabulary ADR (`adr-2026-08-16`) already established the pattern:
  closed, corpus-validated sets, bound by an integrity check.
- **Dispositions suppress findings**, so identity must not over-match: an identity that
  survives a *content* change would let an accepted disposition silently swallow a
  materially different defect at the same location.

## Options Considered

### Option A: Enumerated per-field canonical grammars (status-quo trajectory)

Each anchor field gets a bespoke validated string grammar (path refs, task-id grammar,
test-selector strings, coordinate loci), added as rubrics discover them.

- **Pros:** Fully mechanical; each grammar is precise; incremental delivery.
- **Cons:** The schema is open-ended by construction — the lap-by-lap enumeration and
  unapproved grammar authoring already observed; coordinate-bearing grammars are
  rebase-fragile; every new grammar is an identity-semantics change that invalidates
  existing dispositions.

### Option B: Content-anchored references (closed three-kind schema)

Every anchor reference is exactly one of three canonical kinds, uniform across rubrics;
no other reference kind may be introduced without superseding this ADR.

- **Pros:** Class-level and closed — no future field can demand a new grammar without an
  operator-approved supersession; rebase-stable (content survives a clean rebase;
  coordinates do not); content change ⇒ new identity, which is the correct fail-closed
  narrowness for dispositions; symmetric with the cache's approved content-only identity.
- **Cons:** Content hashes are opaque in reports (mitigated: the canonical payload
  retains the human-readable display string alongside the hash); a conflict-resolved
  rebase that edits hunk

This layer sits *outside* the core router and turns every failure into an improvement opportunity.

### What it does

```
Every message flows through the pipeline → produces a trace
↓
Case Review watches for failures:
  • FAQ abstentions (customer asked something KB doesn't cover)
  • Low-confidence escalations (router unsure, escalated to human)
  • Churn risk flags (angry customer, fast-tracked to human)
  • Guardrail blocks (PII, injection, fraud attempts)
  • Fallback usage (system had to degrade gracefully)
↓
Analytics Dashboard shows 24-hour metrics:
  • Messages tested vs. cases reviewed (the gap = potential)
  • Knowledge-base gaps by frequency (what customers ask, bot can't answer)
  • Escalation breakdown (why customers went to humans)
↓
KB Suggestion Engine:
  • Detects FAQ abstentions
  • Auto-generates doc skeletons
  • Human writes the answer → system re-indexes
  • Next customer with same question gets instant answer
↓
Replay & Metrics:
  • Run 10-ticket test before/after improvement
  • Measure: cost, latency, escalation rate, resolution rate
  • Prove ROI of adding a KB doc or tuning a threshold
↓
Governance & Red-Team:
  • Run 6 security tests: IDOR, injection, PII, spoofing, social eng, churn
  • Validate ownership checks, guardrail blocks, policy limits
```

### How this helps CX (practical view)

**For customers:**
- **Faster answers** — KB gets better coverage. Today customer waits 5 min for human; tomorrow same question gets instant answer.
- **No repeated problems** — When one customer triggers a gap, the system flags it. Next customer with the same issue gets the answer.
- **Protected privacy** — PII detection blocks credit cards from logs. Security tests prevent IDOR attacks.
- **Immediate help when needed** — Churn risk detection sends angry customers straight to a human instead of bot runaround.

**For the company:**
- **Visibility into failures** — See which questions the bot can't answer; which escalations are happening.
- **Measurable improvement** — Replay tests prove that adding a KB doc actually reduces escalations + cost.
- **Safe iteration** — Red-team tests catch regressions (IDOR blocks still working? PII still redacted?).
- **Compliance** — Full audit trail, ownership checks, policy limits in code.

### The dashboard (QA Suite)

Run `uvicorn server:app --port 8000` and explore:

- **🧪 Live Testing** — Chat interface with real-time decision trace (intent, confidence, sentiment, cost)
- **📊 Analytics** — Modal dashboard showing 24h metrics, KB gaps, escalations, pending KB suggestions, replay results
- **🔒 Governance** — Modal showing current policy config and red-team test results
- **Vertical switcher** — Test same router across E-Commerce, Banking, Telecom with different KBs and thresholds

* feat(cloudagent): Stage 1 live discovery — confirm a flag against the account, not the snapshot

The AI Cloud Security Engineer reasoned entirely over a snapshot captured before it
started. That is fine for structure (an ARN does not move) but not for the flags a path
actually turns on — a security group left open, a role still holding admin. Those change,
and a stale snapshot is wrong in BOTH directions: a path reported live may already be
closed, and one dismissed as closed may have re-opened. Neither was detectable.

get_resource(id, live:true) now re-reads that resource from the account and answers
AGREES / DIFFERS / COULD NOT CHECK against the snapshot.

The safety envelope was already built and tested — it was simply never reachable. This
wires it: awsfetch's read-only listers (already used by inventory sync) behind an SDK-free
cloudagent.LiveReader, so cloudagent keeps the AWS SDK out of it the same way the
*remediate packages do. Read-only by construction — awsfetch issues only describe/list
verbs and the role is assumed with cloudsafety.SessionPolicy(), which denies mutation
outright, so this cannot become a write path.

The load-bearing distinction is COULD NOT CHECK. An id on a surface that was skipped comes
back not-covered with the reason — never not-found, which the agent would correctly read as
"it was deleted". Concluding a bucket is gone because an API call was never made would drop
a real attack path on the strength of a call that never happened, so awsfetch's existing
Covers()/Coverage() honesty carries all the way into the agent's observation.

It rides on get_resource rather than taking a 13th catalog slot: the ≤12 cap is enforced by
TestToolCatalogStaysWithinTheCap and exists because tool-use accuracy degrades past ~12 —
the same reason estate_context is one tool and not three. (I tried it as its own tool first;
that test caught it.) Appending also puts the graph view and the live view in ONE
observation, so the agent compares them directly.

The account is read ONCE per investigation and cached, so N questions cost one read — what
makes the capability affordable enough to leave enabled. Nil reader (no fetcher wired, or no
connected account) is a real answer: the snapshot is UNCONFIRMED, never "current".

Tested: unread-surface-is-not-absence, read-surface-absence-is-a-deletion, drift detection,
unconfigured/error honesty, reachability through the live flag, and single-read caching.
Mutation-verified (treating an unread surface as covered compiles and fails the test).

* fix(runner): run L1.5 on the ENGINE scan path — the product's primary path skipped it

Researching whether a human security engineer can actually use this product surfaced a
defect far bigger than the UI gaps I went looking for.

The L1.5 chain (§11) did NOT run on platform engine scans. Only cmd/tsengine (the CLI)
ever constructed a tracer; there is none in internal/orchestrator or internal/sandbox, and
runner.scanAsset took what the scanner returned and called PutFinding directly. So every
repo, container, web, api and ip scan through the PRODUCT stored findings with:

  - no KEV listing and no EPSS score (the exploited-in-the-wild and patch-priority signals)
  - no exploitability or surface_priority
  - no FP filtering
  - no compliance mapping
  - no corroboration, confidence or verification_status

Meanwhile ~15 secondary ingest paths all call enrichFindings("L1.5 parity §11"). The
asymmetry ran OPPOSITE to what every comment claimed — including enrichFindings' own doc,
which asserted engine findings "already get this via the sandbox tracer", and CLAUDE.md §11,
which said the hooks fire on them "by construction". Both are corrected here.

This is precisely what makes or breaks the audience in question. Practitioners prioritise by
exploited-in-the-wild and triage by confidence; a list with neither is the raw scanner noise
the market says costs more than it saves (organisations willing to rely on AI pentesting fell
to 9% in 2026 from 29%, and 78% report critical false negatives).

Extracts the chain to internal/l15 — its own package because platformapi imports runner (so
runner cannot import back) and it cannot live in internal/tracer (hooks already imports
tracer). platformapi.enrichFindings stays as a thin wrapper so the ingest call sites are
untouched. Also enriches the runner's OWN sync paths (GitHub-org SSPM, OSINT), which were
asymmetric with their HTTP twins for the identical assessor.

The point-in-time score could not answer the question that actually differentiates this —
"is the agent getting worse on MY estate?" — which no public benchmark can answer at all.
It also happens to be the easiest place in the product to lie by accident, because two
percentages will subtract whether or not they measure the same thing.

Two rules, both of which refuse to draw a line rather than draw a misleading one:

  1. One sample is not a trend. Rendering a single run as flat implies a stability nobody

  2. A trend across a CHANGING case set is not comparable. The suite grows every time

breaks comparability even though membership did not change.
