H2: security, supply-chain, incident, and ops gates (21 outcomes) (#135)

* docs: approve the private-preview qualification policy and record H0 reviews

- QUALIFICATION_POLICY: approve private-preview-qualification-v1 (the
  baselines, thresholds, live runs, and H1-H5 gates it defines remain open)
- Fix: the deterministic test provider and recorded fixtures can never satisfy
  the Baseline/Qualification configured-provider identity
- Fix: hard guardrails now explicitly cover non-authoritative projections
  served as authoritative state (invariant 7) and unusable failure states on
  the critical journey (invariant 10)
- PRODUCT_CONTRACT: declare the merged private-preview-v1 envelope current and
  reference the approved qualification policy
- SPEC_CONFORMANCE: record the H0 current-truth, contract/design, and
  adversarial overclaim reviews (fresh-context agent perspectives, pass with
  limitation, not human sign-off) and the remaining gates: make-verify
  dispatch record, required CI on the final commit, and independent human
  maintainer/product/security/accessibility/legal reviews

Limitation: GitHub issue/PR creation and the make-verify dispatch record
require credentials unavailable in this environment; the change is staged on
main for a maintainer to file, push, and dispatch.

* feat: land the extraction-quality-v1 evaluator and corpus (h1-eval)

- tools/h1-eval: recorded mode proves the structural import gate on the
  production splitter, extraction schema, and canon validator, plus corpus and
  rubric integrity and calibration self-consistency; adversarial mutations
  must fail the versioned thresholds (per-category coverage >=80, precision
  >=80, hallucination <=20, zero chronology violations, provenance 100) and
  malformed/unsupported inputs reach their expected bounded error labels
- live mode runs the full two-stage production extraction (character + canon
  prompts) and one OpenAI-compatible judge call, then enforces the same
  thresholds fail-closed; reports record provider/model/SHA and no secrets
- corpus h1-synthetic-v1: Simplified Chinese UTF-8/GBK and English
  UTF-8/BOM-UTF-16 slices, a hostile-instructions case, a mixed-script
  splitter case, five adversarial calibrations, and five malformed labels
- CI runs the recorded gate twice and requires byte-identical reports
- novel-service: derive Clone on ExtractionResult for corpus mutation
- SPEC_CONFORMANCE 5.8: record the landed evaluator; live quality stays
  unqualified

* fix(h1-eval): close adversarial review findings before the gate can claim
extraction-quality-v1 fidelity

- hallucination ceiling rounds up: a true rate above the policy bound can
  never truncate down to a pass
- precision and hallucination now divide recorded-side matches by recorded
  facts; coverage stays expected-side per category
- live mode enforces chronology deterministically (event sequence against
  the expected table), runs the production chunk-scan/merge path, verifies
  first appearances against split chapters, and omits unverifiable
  characters like the production handler
- adversarial cases declare the exact threshold they must trip (coverage,
  precision/hallucination, provenance, chronology) and the gate asserts the
  mechanism, so a structural failure cannot masquerade as calibration
- corpus composition minimums per class and per failure mechanism keep the
  gate non-vacuous
- README claims now match what each mode proves; decode and oversized
  rejection evidence is attributed to the novel-service tests that own it

* feat: drill the S3 source-boundary kill/restart recovery (H1)

- docker-compose.s3-e2e.yml: MinIO plus bucket init and S3 source
  retention for novel-service, so the drill runs the real retained-object
  replay path
- tests/e2e/source_recovery_drill.sh: parks the source-stage replay at its
  fenced chapter commit with a drill-held EXCLUSIVE lock on chapters, then
  hard-kills novel-service there, restarts it, and verifies exact resume
  from the retained object (chapter content hashes equal the uploaded
  source), one character, one canon, budget compliance, zero provider calls
  for completed work, and a 409 on ready retry; --self-test mutation checks
  keep the verifier honest; two consecutive local runs pass
- ci.yml: self-check plus a dedicated S3 topology cycle for the drill
- ROADMAP, PRODUCT_CONTRACT, and SPEC_CONFORMANCE record the landed
  evidence; the remaining live-evidence gaps are unchanged

Local verification ran against the gateway port (127.0.0.1:18081) because
this host has port 80 occupied; CI exercises the same drill through Nginx.

* fix(source-drill): close adversarial review findings

- verifier and self-test share one module (tests/e2e/source_recovery_verify.py)
  so the mutation checks cannot drift from the runtime checks
- drop the hardcoded kill_stage record field; the live DB assertions at kill
  time remain the boundary proof
- wait for persisted avatars to settle before the completed-work provider-call

- the extraction prompt now requests the full 5.5 dimension set: setting

- unit tests cover the cap, prominence retention, the exact summary length

- SPEC_CONFORMANCE: the cap and the 2000-character bound move to Verified;

  instrumented run_body wrapper created AFTER the subscriber init, so the
  span re-enters on every poll and covers startup, shutdown, and request

feat: Agents — send one conversation to an assistant that is not on this machine (#46)

* feat: Agents — send one conversation to an assistant that is not on this machine

Turing's own assistant stays the default and the only local one. Agents adds
the ability to configure Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok or any OpenAI-compatible
endpoint, and to hand a chosen conversation to one of them.

Routing is per conversation and only ever by hand. Nothing is inferred and
nothing is global: a conversation goes where someone sent it, and every other
conversation stays here. The destination is read inside the same transaction
that accepts the message and frozen into the job payload, so re-pointing or
deleting an agent cannot redirect a message already sent — it must not be
possible for a transcript to arrive at a company the user did not pick.

Because this is the one feature that breaks the local-first promise on purpose,
it says so where the user is looking rather than in a settings screen:

  - A strip above the conversation names the destination at all times, and
    turns amber with "messages leave your machine" when that destination is off
    it. A failed read says it does not know, never "stays on your machine" —
    reassurance after a failed read is the one lie that strip exists to prevent.
  - Each routed message writes a notice into the transcript itself, naming the
    agent, the endpoint host and the model, in the same transaction that queues
    the run.
  - Cross-session recall is disabled for routed runs. The user opted ONE
    conversation into leaving; recall draws on conversations they never chose to
    send anywhere, and widening consent silently is exactly the surprise the
    first commitment forbids. Capability loses to consent, and the picker says
    so.

Credentials: the database stores a credential NAME, never a key. There is no
column that could hold one, and a test asserts that. The keys live in
TURING_AGENT_API_KEYS in turing-backend/.env — one JSON object of
name -> key — so adding an agent from the client never needs a compose edit.
The agent runtime is the only process that reads the values; the orchestrator
parses the same variable but keeps only the names, which is enough to tell the
client an agent will not work yet instead of letting them find out by sending a
message. No key is ever written to SQLite, put on a job payload, sent over the
runtime stream, or handed to a client.

All four vendors expose an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint, so this
is the existing openai_compatible provider configured per job — one client, not
four integrations. A plaintext http endpoint is refused unless it is on this
machine, since the whole conversation travels over that URL.

Left unwired, a routed job fails with external_agent_unavailable rather than
being answered locally under another assistant's name; a missing key fails with
a message naming the credential and the file it belongs in.

* fix: act on the pre-push review of the Agents feature

Two findings were real defects, not polish.

**A base URL could smuggle an API key into the database.** `https://user:sk-secret@host/v1` passed every check — absolute, https, has a host, no query, no fragment — and Go's HTTP client turns that userinfo into an Authorization header, so it is a working credential. It would have been written to `external_agents.base_url`, copied into every job payload, put on the runtime stream, and handed back to any client that lists agents, which is precisely what the credential design exists to prevent. Rejected at the only door into that column, with a message that points at TURING_AGENT_API_KEYS and does not echo the key that was pasted.

**The egress notice was written in the past tense before any egress happened.** "Sent to X — this message left your machine" went into the transcript inside the enqueue transaction, when the job is only queued. It is false on every designed failure path: a missing API key or unwired runtime fails the run before a provider is chosen, a debug tool command is answered locally, and a cancelled or unclaimed run never reaches a vendor. This project ranks a false statement to the user above every other kind of defect. Now worded prospectively — "Sending to X — this message leaves your machine" — which is true in both outcomes, and a test refuses the past tense.

Routing now leaves an audit record. `session.routed` carries the agent, endpoint host and model; `session.unrouted` records the return to local, and only when something actually changed, so no-op clears do not bury the real decisions. Writing that record in the same transaction as the routing surfaced a deadlock the review did not: the FK-violation probe read through the pool while the transaction held the pool's single connection. It is probed on the transaction now, and the existing "which side is missing" test is what hung.

Also, from the review: the picker sheet joined the overflow matrix and immediately failed at 568x320 — its fixed heading left no room for the choices on a landscape phone, so the heading scrolls with them; the bar renders "Checking where this conversation goes" instead of nothing while it loads, since an absent strip reads as reassurance the failure branch deliberately refuses to give; `credential_available` is a startup snapshot, so the client now says to restart the backend; the endpoint helper names host.docker.internal, which is the one that reaches a local gateway from a container; over-long URLs and credential names get errors that describe the actual problem; and the four copies of the agent column list and scan are one.

The tool policy for a routed run is now pinned by a test rather than left implicit. Recall is suppressed because it draws on other conversations the user never chose to send anywhere; the tools stay because they act on this conversation at this user's request, with mutations still gated by the approval token. Reversing that should mean editing a test.

New tests cover: userinfo in a base URL, the notice's tense, the audit rows, renaming an agent onto another's name, a resolver target with no endpoint, a nil target, a routed job surviving a requeue onto attempt two, and the picker sheet at 320/360/568.

* feat(orgs): OrganizationInvitation + OrganizationMember entities

The `OrganizationMember` / `OrganizationInvitation` pair that
docs/specs/features/tenants-and-organizations/spec.md §7 defers to v1.1.
Entities and registration only — no behaviour yet.

🛑 organization_members is the ROSTER, not the authorization check. Access
stays `user.tenantId === organization.tenantId` via
OrganizationMembershipService.ensureMember, unchanged. Five independent read
paths depend on that equality (ensureMember, OrganizationService.listForUser,
ScopeOwnershipGuard, TeamsService.listOrgUsers, TeamsService.addMember), and
rewriting them is a far larger change than adding invitations. The table
answers what tenant-equality cannot: who invited this person, when they
joined, and for which Organization — and it is the seam a future per-Org
permission model tightens without a second migration.

Two deliberate tightenings versus the WorkInvitation template:

  - `email` is NOT NULL. WorkInvitation.email is nullable because a Work
    invite can be a bare link handed over out of band. An Org invite exists
    to reach someone with no account, and the mail path silently no-ops on a
    null recipient — nullable would make "invited someone unreachable"
    representable.
  - A partial unique index on (organizationId, emailNormalized) WHERE
    status = 'pending'. Without it, clicking invite twice mints two
    independently redeemable tokens for one mailbox and revoking the visible
    one leaves the other live. Partial, so re-inviting after a revoke or an
    expiry stays legal.

`emailNormalized` is stored rather than derived because the uniqueness index
and the accept-time comparison must agree on one canonical form; computing it
in two places is how "already invited" and "not invited" end up both true.

ORGANIZATION_MEMBER_ROLES has exactly one value on purpose.
OrganizationMembershipService.ensureAdmin is currently
`return this.ensureMember(...)` and its docblock forbids adding a role check
without a product decision, so shipping an `admin` option would put a control
in the UI that grants nothing.

writer of users.tenantId in the codebase and the only one that ever points a
user at a Tenant somebody else owns, so it lives beside ensureTenant to keep
every write to that column in one audited file.

🛑 It will NOT move a user between Tenants. Hard refusal, not best-effort,
for four independent reasons:

  1. Every row the user already created is stamped with their OLD tenantId by
     ScopeStampingSubscriber and by createOrganization. Repointing orphans all
     of it — the rows keep the old tenant, so their whole history silently
     vanishes from the scope they can now see. Data loss without a DELETE.
  2. tenants.ownerUserId is UNIQUE, so an owner cannot cleanly stop owning;
     repointing leaves an owner-linked, member-less orphan Tenant.
  3. listForUser returns every Org of user.tenantId, so repointing instantly
     hides all of their own Organizations from them.
  4. The FK on users.tenantId is ON DELETE SET NULL — there is no
     database-level protection. The guard must be in code, and tested.

backfill: dragging an invitee's pre-existing private rows into the inviter's

because WorkRepository filters on userId, never tenantId.

* fix(orgs): boot crash + two ways an invitee could gain unrevocable access

Three defects found by an adversarial review of this branch, all confirmed by
reading the code rather than taken on trust.

1. CRITICAL — the API would have crash-looped at boot.
   OrganizationsModule declares a controller using @UseGuards(AuthSessionGuard)
   but never imported AuthModule. AuthModule is NOT @Global and
   AuthSessionGuard uses constructor injection, so Nest cannot resolve it —
   "Nest can't resolve dependencies", every pod, on startup. TeamsModule
   imports it for exactly this reason. tsc cannot see this, and my own
   module-wiring spec missed it because it only checked the flow service's
   paramtypes, not the controller's guards.

2. HIGH — accept() granted access before claiming the token.
   joinTenant COMMITS users.tenantId, and only then did tryAccept run the
   conditional UPDATE. If a revoke landed in that window the claim failed, the
   code threw, and nothing rolled back: the invitee kept TENANT-WIDE access
   with no roster row — invisible in the members list (which reads the roster)
   and not removable via removeMember (which needs one). A revoked invitation
   still granted access.

   My docblock argued for that ordering. It was wrong: it reasoned only about
   the refusal case and never considered a successful join followed by a lost
   claim. Whatever gate authorizes access has to be the atomic one, so the
   claim now runs FIRST and the grant only happens if it wins.

   The double-click path is also now precise — it checks
   acceptedByUserId === userId instead of inferring "it was me" from a failed
   re-read, which previously also matched a REVOKED invitation and reported
   success for it.

3. HIGH — joinTenant's check-then-update was a TOCTOU.
   Two invitations accepted at the same instant both observed
   `tenantId IS NULL` and both wrote, homing the user in whichever tenant
   committed last while BOTH invitations were marked accepted. Now a
   conditional UPDATE (UserRepository.claimTenantIfUnassigned,
   WHERE "tenantId" IS NULL) lets the database arbitrate; losing to the SAME
   tenant is idempotent success, losing to a different one is the existing
   refusal.

* fix(auth): register now returns you to where you were headed

The "create an account" half of every organization invitation was a dead end.
The landing page stores /org-invite/<token> in redirect_url and sends a brand
new person here to sign up — and `register` never consulted the cookie, so it
dropped them on the dashboard with the invitation unaccepted and no longer
reachable from anywhere in the UI. Registration is the ONLY way an invited
outsider gets an account, so this broke the core journey the whole feature
exists for. `login` has honoured the cookie all along.

🛑 Ordering matters, and I got it wrong first: `getRedirectUrl` REPLACES the
href wholesale when a cookie is present, so appending the EW-077
unverified-email notice before it meant the notice was silently dropped for
exactly the users who followed a stored link — invited newcomers, the group
most likely to have an unconfirmed address. The notice is now applied AFTER
the destination resolves, so it survives whichever one wins. That regression
was caught by the existing EW-077 spec, not by me.

getRedirectUrl validates the stored value (relative or allow-listed host
only), so this cannot become an open redirect.

* fix(orgs): members list showed UUIDs and offered you a button that evicts you

Two review findings with one root cause: the members endpoint returned bare
userIds, so the UI had nothing to render and no way to tell which row was the
person looking at it.

  - The roster rendered `m.userId`, i.e. a raw UUID. Unusable for the one
    decision the list exists to support — deciding who to remove.
  - The "is this me?" check compared against a `currentUserId` prop that the
    parent NEVER PASSED. It was always undefined, so no row ever matched, and
    every member was offered a Remove button on their own row. Clicking it
    deletes your roster row and, if it was your last membership in the tenant,
    clears your users.tenantId — evicting you from every organization in the
    workspace, with no undo in the UI.

listMembers now resolves each row to a person and returns `username`, `email`
and a SERVER-COMPUTED `isSelf`. Computing isSelf server-side is the point: the
caller's identity is already known there, and a client that has to be told its
own id separately is a client that will one day forget to — which is exactly
what happened. The `currentUserId` prop is gone rather than left as a trap.

`username` is what `resolveMemberViews` already uses for team rosters, so the
same person reads the same way in both places. userId survives only as the
last-resort fallback if the User row has genuinely vanished.

* fix(orgs): keep the invitation token out of URLs, logs and Sentry

The public preview took the token as a query parameter, so the full 64-hex
tenant-granting credential appeared in the request URL — and this repo
persists URLs in two places:

  - logging.interceptor.ts logs `Incoming Request: ${method} ${originalUrl}`,
    which its own comment notes is forwarded on as $log events.
  - Sentry attaches `event.request.url`, query string included, to transaction
    events. Its scrubber only matches pathnames under `/auth`, so
    /api/org-invite/preview was not covered.

That defeated the design outright. The database stores only sha256(token)
precisely so the plaintext exists in exactly one place — the email body — and
a token in a URL undoes that with no other change required.

Preview is now a POST carrying the token in the body, which neither of those
two paths captures. A POST for a read is deliberate, and the same shape token
introspection endpoints use.

* fix(orgs): write the roster row BEFORE granting access, not after

accept() makes three separate commits with no enclosing transaction —
joinTenant writes through a different repository — so some partial state is
unavoidable. The real choice is which partial state to prefer, and the
deciding property is VISIBILITY.

Previously the grant came first, so a failing roster write left the person
with TENANT-WIDE ACCESS and no roster row: invisible in the members list, and
removeMember refuses with `not_a_member` because there is no row to delete.
That is precisely the unrevocable state this method was already fixed once to
avoid, reachable through a second door.

Reversed, the worst case is a roster row with no access: the person shows up
in the members list, an admin can see and remove them, and re-accepting
repairs it. Harmless and self-announcing.

recordMembership is idempotent, so writing it first costs nothing on the
happy path. The duplicate call after the grant is gone.

* fix(orgs): an expired invitation no longer blocks re-inviting that person forever

The partial unique index is WHERE status = 'pending', and NOTHING moves a row
from pending to expired on a timer — expireBefore exists but nobody calls it.
So an invitation that aged out still occupies the slot: re-inviting the same
address fails with `invitation_already_pending`, telling the admin there is a
live invitation when the token behind it is dead.

That was permanent. The pending-invitations list would show it, but revoking
is the only lever and revoking an invitation you were told is pending — in
order to send the same person the same invitation — is not a step anyone
would guess at.

issue() now retires the aged-out row for that one (organization, email) pair
before inserting. Scoped rather than a table sweep, so issuing an invitation
stays a bounded write, and best-effort (.catch) so a sweep failure cannot
block a legitimate invite — the index still protects correctness either way.

Verified: 20/20. Control: removing the sweep fails exactly the new test, which
also asserts the sweep happens BEFORE the insert — the other order would be
rejected by the index first and prove nothing.

* fix(orgs): a failed invitation email no longer strands an unusable pending row

The invitation row commits before the mail call, and the raw token exists in
exactly one place — that email. So a send failure left a row whose token
reached NOBODY and which cannot be recovered, because the database holds only
sha256.

Left pending, that row is worse than useless: the partial unique index on
(organizationId, emailNormalized) WHERE status='pending' BLOCKS re-inviting
the address, and there is no resend endpoint. The admin is told an invitation
is pending for a token that does not exist anywhere, and the obvious
response — send it again — is refused.

invite() now revokes the invitation when the send fails, releasing the address
immediately so retrying works, and rethrows so the caller reports the failure
instead of claiming an invite went out. The revoke is best-effort: a secondary
failure while tidying up must not replace the mail error, which is the one the
admin actually needs to see.

New spec, 5/5, with two controls: a successful send must NOT revoke (or the
main assertion would pass for the wrong reason), and removing the revoke call
fails exactly the one test — verified by counting occurrences before and after
arming, 1 -> 0, because a control that quietly fails to arm looks identical to
a passing one.

production database), then fixes the real bugs that surfaced once the

  table that was never actually used by auth.

  meant "replace" actually inserted a duplicate row).

Authentication Bypass For Endpoints With Anonymous Access

Using a remember-me cookie with an arbitrary username can cause Opencast
to assume proper authentication for that user even if the remember-me
cookie was incorrect given that the attacked endpoint also allows
anonymous access.

This way, an attacker can, for example, fake a remember-me token, assume
the identity of the global system administrator and request non-public
content from the search service without ever providing any proper
authentication.

The reason for this problem is that using a remember-me cookie will
always cause the user in the request context to be populated, even if
the cookie is invalid by now. This is usually no problem, except in
combination with anonymous access where anonymous authentication is
granted and the request may continue.

In such a case, Opencast's security service would just check that a user
existed in the request context and assume proper authentication of this
user, never checking if it's actually anonymous authentication.

This patch adds this additional check, falling back to the anonymous

<Callout type="info" title="The route is opt-in">
Omit `attachmentStaging` and no upload surface is exposed — a client sends already-staged `MessageAttachment` references directly on `chat`. `attachmentStores.memory()` covers tests and dev (it `data:`-encodes the bytes); a real deployment binds its own store presigning against S3/GCS or wrapping the host's media pipeline.

A request targets an agent by name via the `agent` field on `POST /agent/chat` (omit it for the default). Model, store, sink, and governance are shared across all agents; each definition overrides only its own prompt, tools, personas, `defaultPersona`, `modelId`, and `maxSteps`.

## Multi-agent delegation

`delegatesTo` declares which other agents an agent may hand work to. For each edge, the provider **synthesizes an `agent`-kind delegate tool** named `ask_<target>` (non-alphanumeric characters become underscores). The orchestrator calls it like any tool — `ask_researcher({ task: '...' })` — and the loop runs the target agent and feeds its answer back. You never write the delegate handler; the loop handles delegation itself.

<Callout type="info" title="How a delegate tool is named and described">
`delegateToolName('researcher')` → `ask_researcher`. Its description is auto-generated ("Delegate a task to the 'researcher' agent and get its answer.") and, when the target has a flat-string base prompt, that prompt is appended so the orchestrator's model knows what the specialist is for. Its input is a zero-dependency `{ task: string }` Standard Schema — synthesizing delegate tools never pulls in Zod.
</Callout>

Under the **inline runner**, delegation runs as a nested in-process loop on a transient sub-thread. Because a nested sub-agent has no human to prompt, its `action` tools are auto-declined rather than left hanging — so keep human-approval actions on the top-level agent. Under the **durable runner**, the same delegation maps to a tracked durable child workflow (`ctx.child`). See the [agent loop](/docs/agent/concepts/agent-loop) and [The durable runner](/docs/agent/durability/durable-runner).

fix: close the 2026-08-18 audit — authorizable delegation, live actor directory, typed dashboard config, and docs that match the code (#71)

* fix(deps): restore engines.node to a range and stop renovate re-pinning it

Both published packages carried an exact `engines.node` (`v22.23.2` for the
agent, `v26.7.0` for the dashboard) rather than a range, so every consumer on
any other Node version got an unsupported-engine warning on install — and a
hard failure under `engine-strict`.

The cause was renovate: #45 ("pin dependencies") rewrote
`">=22.0.0 <23"` into `"v22.23.2"`, because `renovate.json` sets
`rangeStrategy: "pin"` globally and nothing excluded `engines` from it.
Pinning a dependency is the point of that setting; pinning the
supported-runtime range is a category error, so `engines` is now opted out
and the bot cannot re-pin it next cycle.

Set both to `>=20.6.0` — the floor `@adonisjs/core` v7 itself requires, and
what the rest of the Agora packages publish.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(agent): let a delegatesTo edge declare the roles/ability it needs

A synthesized `ask_<target>` delegate tool goes through the same `RolesPolicy`
gate as every other tool — correctly, since delegation is a capability like any
other. But the spec carried neither `roles` nor `ability`, and there was no way
to put them there: under `DefaultToolAuthorizer` that made every delegation
ADMIN-only, and under `authzToolAuthorizer` (which denies any tool with no
declared ability) it made delegation *unreachable*, with no configuration that
could open it.

`delegatesTo` now accepts `{ agent, roles?, ability? }` alongside the bare
string, and `registerDelegateTools` copies the annotation onto the synthesized
spec. A bare string is unchanged and still fail-closed — that stays the default
so an unannotated edge is never silently more permissive than the tools around it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(agent): resolve actor display labels on the governance surfaces

`actorDirectory` was configurable, documented, and dead: the provider resolved
it into a private field that was written at boot, cleared at shutdown, and never
read. `ActorDirectory.resolveDisplay` had zero call sites outside its own test,
so every governance surface rendered raw opaque refs no matter what an app bound.

Every governance route that returns an `actorRef` now also returns an optional
`actorLabel`, decorated at the HTTP boundary from ONE batched directory lookup
over the distinct refs in the page — not one lookup per row, which is what turns
a 200-row page into 200 queries against the host's user table.

The field is omitted (never null, never a copy of the ref) when the directory
knows no label, so `actorLabel ?? actorRef` stays the single rendering rule. An
unbound or throwing directory leaves the rows exactly as the read-model produced
them: a display label is never worth failing a governance page over.

Also corrects the `AgentGovernanceQueries` cost formula docblock, which
predated cache-token pricing and claimed the full input was billed at the input
rate.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(agent): type the dashboard block on AgentConfig

The console's config lives at `agent.dashboard`, but `AgentConfig` had no such
field — the provider read it through an untyped `config.get('agent.dashboard')`
string path. So the documented usage, `defineConfig({ dashboard: {...} })`, was
an excess-property error: the one call site the type exists to check was the one
place it didn't.

Declare `dashboard?: AgentDashboardConfig` on `AgentConfig` and have the provider
read it off the typed object. Also documents the real attachment allow-list
default, which is an exact-match list of seven content types rather than the
"common images + application/pdf + text/*" the docblock claimed (`text/markdown`
has always been a 415).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(agent): translate the published source's JSDoc to English

Six files under `src/` carried Portuguese doc comments — and one carried
Portuguese in a thrown error message — all of which ship in `dist/` and surface
in every consumer's editor tooltips. The libraries are English-facing; this is
the convention catching up with the code.

Also drops two NestJS-era references left in `types.ts`
(`@dudousxd/nestjs-agent-authz`, `AgentModule.forFeature([...])`) and the
`stores/factory.ts` note claiming pgvector and memory are the only retrievers,
which predates the Qdrant backend sitting directly below it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(agent): document the shipped surface, and stop denying half of it

The audit found the docs contradicting the code in three directions at once:
features documented as absent that ship, features not documented at all, and
copy-paste examples that throw.

**Three pages said the React client does not exist.** It is published — the
`./client` and `./react` subpaths, ~20 exports. `streaming-and-http.mdx` told
readers to install `@dudousxd/nestjs-agent-react` (another ecosystem's package)
and described a hook result that is not the real one; `generative-ui.mdx` said

`browser-client.mdx` covers both subpaths, including the two things the client
deliberately does NOT do — approvals, and stopping the server-side run on
`cancel()`.

**MCP was entirely invisible** — zero occurrences in the docs, despite two export
subpaths, a published config stub, five routes, an auth model, and a hard
dependency on `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`. New page `mcp.mdx`.

**`governance/telescope.mdx` described the opposite of the code.** Its callout
claimed "entirely entry-backed — no read-model"; the tab has nine sections, 19
governance-backed providers and four RAG ones. Rewritten, with the extension API
(`providers`/`sections`, the reserved `agent.` prefix that throws, the deep-link
templates, the panel/SDK types).

Correctness fixes, each verified against the code:

- `redis-streaming.mdx` named the peer `@adonis-agora/redis` three times; it is
  `@adonisjs/redis`. Added the missing `ttlSeconds`.
- `stores/lucid.mdx` presented `autoCreateTables` as opt-in; it is on by default.
- `testing.mdx` ran `TextDecoder` over `subscribe()`, which yields `StreamFrame`

- `governance/dashboard.mdx` showed a `dashboard: {}` block that did not
  type-check (now it does, see the sibling commit) and a `node ace add` for a
  package with no configure hook. It also called a console with approve/reject
  and a pricing editor "read-only".
- `governance/read-model.mdx` claimed omitting `governanceQueries` disables the

- `governance/quota-and-cost.mdx` gave a cost formula that ignored cache tokens,
  claimed `bump` increments every turn when the recommended ledger store makes it
  a no-op (double-counting for anyone who followed it), said the quota route
  returns the remaining budget, and promised `null` costs that rollups return as 0.
- `governance/authorization.mdx` promised a thrown `authorize` message in the 403;

- `governance/authz-bouncer.mdx` used a bare `app` with no import.
- `retrieval/rag.mdx` called `actor.roles.map` unguarded on an optional field.
- `getting-started.mdx` said `configure` publishes one migration; it publishes three.

New pages for public API that had none: Qdrant, the corpus lifecycle
(`updateMetadata`/`listDocumentIds`/`removeWhere` and the guard that refuses
`removeWhere({})`), diagnostics (all eight event names and four span channels,
including the two that are declared but never emitted), and the programmatic API
(`AgentService` from a job — and what it does not enforce).

Dropped `roadmap.mdx`: it was release notes with an internal codename in user

Removed the version-history prose ("published as 0.12.0", "shipped in 0.12.0",

changelog is where a version lives.

user-manageable via the `/roles` screen; only the seeded `super_admin` role (constant in
`lib/constants/roles.ts`, never a raw string) is protected from rename/delete/deactivation.
`/roles` and `/users` are gated two ways: `components/Layout/Sidebar.tsx` hides the nav items unless

deactivated after a token was issued.

Generate new passwords in a secure way

Previously, lost passwords were generated via
org.apache.commons.lang.RandomStringUtils,
which is using java.util.Random internally.

This PRNG is has a 48-bit seed, that can easily be bruteforced
if an attacker is able to get the PRNG's output, for example
but resetting their own account multiple times,
leading to trivial privileges escalation attacks.

This commit makes use of java.security.SecureRandom
instead.

explanation:
Fix three production-blocking bugs, unify the audit data model, build real reports

Found by walking the audit lifecycle on a new local emulator harness. All three
failures were silent in production and none had a visible symptom pointing at the
real cause.

PRODUCTION BUGS

1. Annual-plan approval was dead. firestore.rules exceeded Firestore's hard ceiling
   of 1000 expression evaluations per request, and Firestore reports an overrun as
   PERMISSION_DENIED - indistinguishable from a real authorization failure, so the
   UI blamed the network. The /annualPlans update rule ORed five branches that each
   re-derived the caller through isQualityStaff()/isSelf()/isAdmin()/appUserId(),
   every one of which re-runs isActive() and its four document reads. The caller is
   now resolved once at the allow and passed down as parameters.

2. Onboarding could never complete. clearsOwnPasswordChangeFlag() was written and
   documented but never referenced in any allow, so an employee onboarded with an
   access code could set a password and never clear the flag saying they owed one -
   every later sign-in demanded the change again, forever.

3. Sign-out was never recorded. signOutUser() logged the event before signOut() "on
   purpose", but did not await it, so the write raced the auth token and lost. The
   one event an append-only log most needs to show was missing from all of them.

AUTHORIZATION

- /audits allow update was `if isActive()` - any of the company's employees could
  rewrite any audit, findings and answers included. Now the quality department, the
  audit team, and the audited department's auditee.
- New external_auditor role: read everywhere, write nowhere, enforced centrally.

DATA MODEL

Two different Audit interfaces existed - one in @/types, one in @/lib/firestore -
disagreeing on whether currentStage was a number or a string, invisible because
nothing imported the first. Unified onto what is actually stored, and the compiler
then found what the drift had been hiding:

- OneDrive attachments were saved without their `type` discriminator
- the audit screen wrote category 'noteworthy' while the audit list rendered
  'opportunity', so every such finding showed a blank category
- 'pending_department_approval' had no label on the audit list
- five leaf types were duplicated across three pages, each subtly different

WORKFLOW

- src/lib/audit-workflow.ts: the three gates the lifecycle turns on - schedule
  confirmation by both parties, checklist approval, and answer approval before the
  auditee is shown anything. Data layer, notifications and activity logging; the
  screens that drive them are not built yet.
- Independence guard: a person can no longer be offered as auditor of their own
  department. It was missing from both the plan editor and the audit wizard.

REPORTS

/reports was a mock - six hard-coded cards and a Download button that called
alert('coming soon'). Now computed from live audits, with working CSV export
(BOM-prefixed so Excel reads the Arabic).

TEST HARNESS

npm run emulator / seed:emulator / dev:emulator - the real org structure against a
local Firebase emulator, with a guard that refuses to run outside a demo- project.
Pinned to JDK 21: firebase-tools 15 refuses anything older, and the Firestore
emulator jar dies on 25.

fix: critical auth bug on pay-app acknowledge + add security headers + fix hydration

Three items in one commit because they're related hardening
that's safer to ship together than in three pieces.

================================================================
ITEM 1: Tenant isolation — /api/pay-apps/[id]/acknowledge
================================================================

Bug (CRITICAL): The public pay-app acknowledge endpoint had
ZERO authentication. Anyone with any payAppId could mark any
pay app as acknowledged by hitting:
  POST /api/pay-apps/<payAppId>/acknowledge
with an empty JSON body.

The intent was that the public /pay-apps/[token] page would
POST to this endpoint when the recipient clicked 'I
acknowledge this draw'. The page is reached via a token
link, no auth required. But the API route never verified
the share token — it just took the payAppId from the URL
and updated the pay app.

This is a cross-pay-app (and effectively cross-tenant)
vulnerability. Knowing one pay app's id (or guessing a
CUID, which is feasible) let you acknowledge any pay app.

Fix: the route now requires a shareToken in the request
body, looks up the pay app by shareToken (NOT by id), and
verifies the URL's payAppId matches the looked-up pay app's
id. Without a valid token: 404. With a valid token but
wrong payAppId: 404 (we don't leak whether the token
exists). With a valid token + matching payAppId: 200.

Also added:
- acknowledgedByEmail / acknowledgedByName on PayApp so
  we record who acknowledged (the previous code didn't
  capture the email the user typed)
- zod validation of the request body (was parsing
  untyped JSON, so a malformed body would 500 the worker)
- Idempotency: re-acknowledging an already-acknowledged
  pay app is a 200 (no-op), preserving the original
  acknowledgedAt timestamp
- 409 Conflict for PAID pay apps (you can't re-acknowledge
  after the wire has cleared)

Regression tests at app/api/pay-apps/[id]/acknowledge/
__tests__/acknowledge.test.ts cover:
  - no body
  - missing token
  - too-short token
  - token not matching any pay app
  - token matches a DIFFERENT pay app (IDOR)
  - DRAFT pay app
  - PAID pay app (409)
  - invalid email
  - valid request → update called correctly
  - idempotent re-acknowledge preserves original timestamp

================================================================
ITEM 2: HTTP security headers (next.config.mjs)
================================================================

The audit agent's main cluster of findings: only HSTS was
present, and it was missing includeSubDomains. Every
other standard header (CSP, X-Frame-Options, nosniff,
Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP/CORP) was
missing entirely. X-Powered-By was leaked.

Added a complete security header set via next.config.mjs
async headers() — applied to every route via /:path*:

  Content-Security-Policy — full policy with allowlisted
    origins for: Clerk, OSM tiles, Nominatim geocoding,
    Vercel Blob, Resend, Clerk image CDN. 'self' for
    default. frame-ancestors 'none' for clickjacking.
    object-src 'none'. 'unsafe-inline' allowed for
    script-src (Next.js streams SSR + Clerk UI needs it)
    and style-src (Tailwind injects styles).

  Strict-Transport-Security — max-age=2y, includeSubDomains,
    preload. Preload is opt-in by submitting to the HSTS
    preload list at hstspreload.org; leaving the directive
    in place doesn't auto-submit.

  X-Frame-Options: DENY — belt-and-braces fallback for
    ancient browsers that don't honor frame-ancestors.

  X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — prevent MIME sniffing.

  Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin —
    don't leak full URLs (with workspace / project IDs) to
    third-party origins.

  Permissions-Policy — allow camera=(self) and
    geolocation=(self) (we use both for Scan + GPS-tagged
    photos); deny everything else including microphone
    (we don't record audio).

  Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
  Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site
    Cross-origin isolation. Required if we ever want to
    use SharedArrayBuffer; cheap insurance today.

  X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off — minor.

  poweredByHeader: false — removed the X-Powered-By
    'Next.js' leak.

Verified with curl -I: every header present on every
response. Build still clean.

================================================================
ITEM 3: Hydration mismatch (React #425 / #422)
================================================================

Root cause: client components computed 'time-ago' strings
inline using Date.now() at render time. The server and
client produced different strings (e.g. '4 min ago' on
server, '5 min ago' on client) → React discards the server
HTML and re-renders on the client (perf hit + flicker +
console exceptions).

Fix: new <RelativeTime iso={...} /> component at
components/ui/RelativeTime.tsx that:
  - Server-renders an ABSOLUTE date (e.g. 'Aug 15') using
    a fixed en-US locale + UTC so the bytes are identical
    on server and first client render
  - On mount, useEffect swaps to the relative form
    ('4 min ago')
  - Re-renders every 30s so '5 min ago' updates while the
    user has the page open
  - Always sets title={iso.toISOString()} on the span
    for accessibility / hover
  - Falls back to 'never' for null/undefined input

Replaced inline relativeTime() calls in:
  - app/(app)/w/[workspace]/team/TeamPageClient.tsx
  - app/(app)/w/[workspace]/scan/ScanPageClient.tsx
  - app/(app)/w/[workspace]/projects/[id]/ProjectLocationBadge.tsx
  - components/messages/MessageThread.tsx
  - components/forms/DraftForm.tsx

Kept the old lib/format/relative-time.ts for the admin
pages (which are server components, no hydration issue)
and for any future server-side rendering need.

fix: restrict folder deletion to the owner or an admin (#27003)

* fix: restrict folder deletion to the owner or an admin

Deleting a folder cascades into the folder owner's chats, messages and the
entire subfolder subtree; the cascade is bound to the folder's owner, not the
caller. The delete handler only enforced owner/admin for root folders.
Subfolder deletion required merely write access, and a write grant on a shared
root folder is inherited by every descendant subfolder. A write-collaborator
could therefore permanently delete the owner's chats by deleting a subfolder of
a shared folder, data they do not own. With delete_contents=false the same path
force-moved the owner's chats out of the folder instead.

This also contradicted the documented sharing model: only the owner or an admin
may delete a shared folder, and write access covers adding and editing chats and
subfolders, not removing the folder.

Because any folder deletion cascades into the owner's data, restrict it to the
owner or an admin for root and subfolders alike, replacing the root/subfolder
split with a single check. Owners and admins are unaffected, and a
write-collaborator can still create, rename and add to shared folders and delete
subfolders they own.

def make_not_authenticated_error(self) -> HTTPException:
    if not request.user.is_authenticated:
        raise PermissionDenied('Authentication required')
        """
        The OAuth 2 specification doesn't define the challenge that should be used,
        because a `Bearer` token is not really the only option to authenticate.

        But declaring any other authentication challenge would be application-specific
        as it's not defined in the specification.

        For practical reasons, this method uses the `Bearer` challenge by default, as
        it's probably the most common one.

        If you are implementing an OAuth2 authentication scheme other than the provided
        ones in FastAPI (based on bearer tokens), you might want to override this.

        Ref: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749
        """
        return HTTPException(
            status_code=HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Not authenticated",
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
        )

    async def __call__(self, request: Request) -> str | None:
        authorization = request.headers.get("Authorization")
        if not authorization:
            if self.auto_error:
                raise self.make_not_authenticated_error()
            else:
                return None
        return authorization

fix(api): close the agent-token gaps found by the codex gate

Critical: the MCP-only rule was scoped to the /api/v1 prefix, so POST /logout —
the one root-level auth:sanctum route — still accepted agent bearers, giving an
agent a human-only action and a token-validity oracle. The refusal now sits on
both route groups; accepting a token is a positive capability exactly one
surface will opt into (#135). The IDOR sweep enumerates every registered route
instead of a prefix, and proves its two exemptions authenticate nothing.

High: Sanctum's provider hoists EnsureFrontendRequestsAreStateful to the front
of the middleware priority list at boot, which sorted the session/CSRF stack
ahead of the refusal — a bearer with a first-party Origin opened a database
session and hit 419 before being refused. AppServiceProvider now hoists the
refusal after Sanctum's provider; asserted on pipeline order and as zero
queries on a rejected request. Mint and its audit record are one transaction;
revoke records through recordSafely and only the request that removed the row
records an event; the Policy trait fails closed on any persistent token that is
not an AgentToken.

Also: no-store on the mint response, a dismiss action for the revealed value,
error-vs-empty on the settings list, deny-as-not-found for a foreign token id,
and a per-member token cap that bounds the unpaginated list.

Dismissals and deferrals recorded in TODOS.md.

[SECURITY] Respect expiration time of password reset token

When a TYPO3 backend user performs a password reset request, a
password reset link including an expiration time is sent to the
user. The expiration time is included in HMAC calculation of
the saved password reset hash, but it is never evaluated if the
expiration time is exceeded.

This change adds the missing validity check for the expiration
time included in the password reset link.

## Broken leg
The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Not authorized to reprice this booking' });
    }

Unauth callers ate a wasted bookingRequests SELECT before hitting a
MISLEADING 403 that suggested a permissions problem, not a
credentials problem. The audit agent classified this as "risky-cosmetic"
because it's a 403→401 client-behavior change; on inspection the reprice
client is always an authenticated logged-in customer, so a 401 only fires
for callers that shouldn't be reaching the endpoint at all.

## Fix (server-only, split into two clean checks)
1. Explicit 401 at the door — before the DB fetch — with an honest
   'Authentication required' message.
2. Ownership check no longer needs the !userId branch — reads cleanly
   as "owner OR verified admin".

Both branches unchanged behaviorally for legitimate callers.

server/tests/reprice-401-hygiene.regression.test.ts — 3 pins:
  ✓ returns 401 explicitly when there is no userId
  ✓ 401 guard sits BEFORE the first db.select() (no wasted round-trip)
  ✓ ownership check no longer folds !userId into the 403 branch

    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  3 passed (3)

None. Completes the auth-slippage sweep on booking-requests.ts —
prior sweep PRs #1904 (confirm), #1911 (7 POSTs), #1912 (GET). This
covers the last remaining router-mounted handler with the same shape.

## Risk
Very low. 401 replaces 403 for anon callers only (a case that already
denied). Legitimate customer + admin repricing unchanged.

Per standing CEO directive.

A self-contained ALARM channel that raises a phone when a real alarm condition
fires in amplifier-work-tracker. Lives in
`src/amplifier_work_tracker/webpush.py`. It adopts the wire shape proven by
Amplifier's notify bundle (`hooks-notify-push`) and adds the three things an
*alarm* channel needs and that bundle lacks: **Bearer auth** for a self-hosted
ntfy, **`Priority: urgent`** (bypasses phone Do-Not-Disturb), and a **bounded
retry + LOUD fail** (never a silent swallow).

## Wire shape

```
POST {NTFY_SERVER}/{NTFY_TOPIC}
Title: <title>
Priority: urgent
Tags: rotating_light,warning
Click: <optional dashboard deep-link>
Authorization: Bearer <NTFY_TOKEN>     # only when a token is configured

<message as raw UTF-8 body bytes>
```

## Configuration (env only — secrets never in a settings file)

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `NTFY_SERVER` | `https://ntfy.sh` | ntfy base URL. Point at your self-hosted instance. |
| `NTFY_TOPIC` | *(unset)* | Topic. On public ntfy.sh the topic name **is** the password — keep it in the env, never a file. |
| `NTFY_TOKEN` | *(unset)* | Self-hosted access token, sent as `Authorization: Bearer`. Optional. |
| `NTFY_ALARM_ENABLED` | *(unset)* | Enable flag (`1`/`true`/`yes`/`on`). Opt-in: while unset, `send_alarm` is a safe no-op. |
| `NTFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | `4` | Retry budget (attempts, not retries). |
| `NTFY_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS` | `0.5` | Base for exponential backoff between attempts. |
| `NTFY_CLICK_BASE` | *(unset)* | Optional dashboard base URL for a `Click:` deep-link back to the item. |

### Why self-hosted + token (recommended for this deployment)

This deployment runs behind Tailscale. A private self-hosted ntfy plus an
access token removes the "topic name == password" fragility of public ntfy.sh:
the topic can no longer be guessed off the wire, and delivery is authenticated.

## Retry + LOUD fail semantics

- **2xx** → delivered.
- **Transient** (network/timeout error, HTTP `429`, or any `5xx`) → retried up
  to `NTFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS` with exponential backoff.
- **Exhausted retries, or a non-transient `4xx`** → `logger.error(...)` **and**
  `AlarmDeliveryError`. The `logger.error` is deliberately NOT debug-only (the
  way `hooks-notify-push` logs) — it is the line that must appear in the journal
  when the phone did not ring.
- **Disabled** (`NTFY_ALARM_ENABLED` not truthy) → no-op result, so call sites
  can invoke it unconditionally.

## The trigger — bound to the already-trusted signal

The alarm keys off the **custody-TTL breach**, i.e. the exact signal the reaper
already trusts: `custody.reclaim_eligible(record) -> (eligible, reason)`. It
does **not** re-decide eligibility and is **not** wired to any new/unproven
ranking logic. Helpers in `webpush.py`:

- `reclaim_alarm_payload(item_id, holder, reason)` — pure `(title, message, tags, click)` formatting.
- `alarm_for_reclaimed_item(item_id, holder, reason, ...)` — async, formats + sends (urgent).
- `fire_reclaim_alarm(item_id, holder, reason, config=None)` — **sync, never-raises** entry point for the reap-sweep worker thread.

additive.

Frontend nginx config is `frontend/nginx.conf.template`, rendered by the image's envsubst entrypoint from `${PORT}` (Cloud Run) and `${BACKEND_HOST}` (the origin `/sitemap.xml` proxies to — update it if the backend service is renamed, or the proxy 502s). This replaced the old `sed`-the-port-at-runtime hack. It also 301s the `*.run.app` hostnames to `timetify.net`, so testing a deploy on its raw Cloud Run URL will bounce you to production — hit the custom domain, or check `Host`-specific behaviour with an explicit header. Full rules in [SEO](seo.md).

**nginx `add_header` inheritance.** A `location` that declares *any* `add_header` silently drops every server-level one — which previously would have removed the CSP and HSTS headers from exactly the HTML responses that need them. The document locations therefore use `expires -1` instead of `add_header Cache-Control`; the asset locations, which do need `add_header` for `immutable`, repeat `X-Content-Type-Options` explicitly. Adding an `add_header` to a location means re-adding the security headers there too.

## Signed media URLs (post-pentest)

Media is served through **signed, expiring URLs** (`main/storage.py`, `SignedGoogleCloudStorage`), not a public bucket. Two things must be true in the environment or media breaks:

1. **The bucket must not be public.** `gsutil iam ch -d allUsers:objectViewer gs://$GS_BUCKET_NAME`. Leaving the binding in place is not merely redundant — it re-opens anonymous `storage.objects.list`, so the whole bucket stays enumerable regardless of signing.
2. **The runtime service account must be able to sign via the IAM API.** django-storages (≤1.14.6) signs with a local private key, which Cloud Run's metadata credentials do not have; `SignedGoogleCloudStorage` instead signs through IAM `signBlob`, which needs the SA to hold `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` **on itself**:

   ```
   gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding "$SA_EMAIL" \
       --member="serviceAccount:$SA_EMAIL" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator"
   ```

If signing fails the backend logs `gcs.signing_failed` at ERROR and falls back to an unsigned URL, so a missing binding degrades instead of 500ing — but that fallback only *works* while the bucket is still public. Treat that log line as "the fix is not actually deployed". URL lifetime is `GS_URL_EXPIRY_SECONDS` (default 2h).

## Other security-relevant env vars

- `ADMIN_URL_PATH` — moves the Django admin off `/admin/`. Set it to something unguessable in prod.
- `TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT` — how many proxies append to `X-Forwarded-For` (default 1, correct for Cloud Run direct). Rate limiting derives the client IP from the *rightmost* N entries, because everything left of them is caller-supplied and forgeable. Raise it if a load balancer is put in front, or per-IP throttling will key on the proxy and limit all users as one.
- `REDIS_URL` — optional. Throttle counters live in the cache; without Redis they fall back to a database cache table (created by migration `0035`). Do **not** let this fall back to a per-process LocMemCache: each Cloud Run instance would get its own budget.
- `THROTTLE_*` — per-endpoint rate overrides; see `REST_FRAMEWORK['DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES']`.

**Migration `0034` can fail on existing data.** It adds case-insensitive unique constraints on username and email. Run `python manage.py find_identity_collisions` first; it lists colliding accounts and exits non-zero, so it can gate the deploy.

def clean_username(self, username, request):
    if not request.user.is_authenticated:
        raise PermissionDenied('Authentication required')
        """
        Allow the backend to clean the username, if the backend defines a
        clean_username method.
        """
        backend_str = request.session[auth.BACKEND_SESSION_KEY]
        backend = auth.load_backend(backend_str)
        try:

def make_not_authenticated_error(self) -> HTTPException:
    if not request.user.is_authenticated:
        raise PermissionDenied('Authentication required')
        """
        The WWW-Authenticate header is not standardized for API Key authentication but
        the HTTP specification requires that an error of 401 "Unauthorized" must
        include a WWW-Authenticate header.

        Ref: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-401-unauthorized

        For this, this method sends a custom challenge `APIKey`.
        """
        return HTTPException(
            status_code=HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Not authenticated",
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "APIKey"},
        )

Fix issues found auditing the codebase, and add CI (#4)

* Fix issues found auditing the codebase

Native core (native/sslocal-ffi):

* `sslocal_last_error` handed out a pointer into the mutex-guarded
  `LAST_ERROR` slot and released the lock before returning, so a
  concurrent `set_last_error` — the core's own tasks record errors —
  could free the buffer while the caller was reading it. The message is
  moved into a slot of its own first; the pointer now stays valid until
  the next `sslocal_last_error` call.
* `sslocal_start_tun_fd` dups the tun descriptor. The tun device closes
  the fd it was given when the runtime is torn down (in the background),
  while `VpnConnection.destroy()` closes the app's; sharing one number
  risked the second close landing on an unrelated descriptor.
* The plugin forwarder's accept loop `continue`d on every error, turning
  a dead listener into a CPU-burning spin. Per-connection failures now
  retry after a back-off, anything else stops the loop.
* `cargo clippy` failed to compile (`not_unsafe_ptr_arg_deref` on
  `sslocal_set_stat_address`); C-string arguments go through one shared
  helper. `cargo fmt` is clean again.
* Unit tests that touch the process-wide state serialize on a lock
  instead of racing each other.
* `net_helper` prints usage instead of panicking on a missing argument.

App (entry/src/main/ets):

* Updating an existing subscription always failed: `SubscriptionStore`
  returned `JSON.parse` output cast to `Subscription`, so `ensureId()`
  was missing and `upsert` threw. Added `fromJson`, mirroring
  `ProfileStore`.
* `JsonStore.remove` called the async `fs.unlink`, whose rejection
  escaped the surrounding try as an unhandled rejection — which
  `TrafficStatsStore.clear` triggers on every VPN start.
* The VPN ability retained every flow-stat connection forever. The core
  opens a new one per 500 ms sample, so the list grew by two entries a
  second for the life of the tunnel; connections are dropped on close.
* Editing a subscription-owned profile dropped its `subscriptionId`, so
  the next subscription update re-added it as a duplicate.
* `Index` never cleared its stats poll timer, which outlived the page.
* `Profile.parseUrl` let a malformed percent escape throw out of the
  parser; in a subscription body one bad entry took the rest with it.
* Store failures in click handlers, a rejected VPN stop, and a
  permission-gated `updateVpnAuthorizedState` no longer surface as
  unhandled rejections.
* The stat endpoint builds a fresh server per port attempt and closes
  the ones that failed to bind.

Scripts:

* `run-tun-e2e-docker.sh` and `build-ohos.sh` expanded empty arrays
  under `set -u`, which aborts on the bash 3.2 that macOS ships — the
  host those scripts exist for. The docker runner also reports a
  missing iproute2 instead of failing with `ip: command not found`.
* `test-e2e-host.sh` numbered its first step 1/2 of 3.
* The on-device e2e's marker URL is a documented constant, not an
  address buried mid-test.

Verified: 30 unit + 2 e2e Rust tests, the OHOS cross-compile check, the
tun packet-routing e2e in Docker, 15 ArkTS unit tests, and both the
default and ohosTest HAP builds.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add CI: run the core tests and all three e2e steps on every push

This repository had no CI at all, and both README.md and AGENTS.md pointed
at a `.github/workflows/harmony.yml` in the parent repo that does not
exist. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` now runs, on every push and pull
request: rustfmt, clippy (`-D warnings`), the Rust unit tests, the SOCKS5
and simple-obfs plugin e2e tunnels, the OpenHarmony cross-compile check,
and the tun packet-routing e2e.

The tun e2e is the notable one — it drives real IP packets through the
tun stack and, until now, could only be run from a privileged container
by hand. A GitHub Linux runner has /dev/net/tun and passwordless sudo, so
`test-e2e-host.sh` now escalates itself instead of requiring the whole
script to run as root, and reports precisely why it skips when it cannot.
The workflow asserts /dev/net/tun exists so a runner change surfaces as a
failure rather than a silent skip.

The Rust crate path-depends on the shared shadowsocks-rust checkout that
lives *outside* this repository, so the workflow clones it to the sibling
path the Cargo manifest expects, at the same v1.23.4 the Android app's
submodule pins.

Also fixed, found while validating the above on Linux:

* `recover_tun_name` cast `c_char` to `u8` unconditionally. `c_char` is
  signed on x86_64 but unsigned on aarch64, so on aarch64-linux the cast
  is a no-op and clippy's `unnecessary_cast` fires — invisible from macOS,
  where that function is not even compiled.
* `run-tun-e2e-docker.sh` always built an x86_64 helper. On an Apple
  Silicon host — the whole reason that script exists — the container ran
  it under qemu emulation, which segfaulted roughly one run in twelve.
  It now builds for the host architecture; 8/8 clean runs after.
* README listed SIP003 plugins as "not ported"; they have been supported
  since 0e264fa.

The ArkTS tests and the HAP build stay out of CI: they need the DevEco
command-line tools, which are not publicly downloadable.

Verified by replaying the whole workflow in a Linux container — clone
step, fmt, clippy, and all three test-e2e-host.sh steps including the tun
e2e as a non-root user via sudo — end to end, exit 0.

  through the server instead.

  instead of hardcoded zeros, rand(), and a disconnected admin_users
  table that was never actually used by auth.
- Fixes silent quiz-publish duplication (missing unique constraint
  meant "replace" actually inserted a duplicate row).

Add the frontend API client and split the types module

Two pieces of foundation that have to exist before any migration slice
branches, because both are files every slice would otherwise edit.

lib/api/client.ts is the single path to the backend. It owns three things
that were each a bug waiting to happen:

  - Base URL, with a NAMED failure. EXPO_PUBLIC_* values are inlined at
    bundle time, so a missing EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL became the literal
    string "undefined" in the URL. React Native reports that as "Network
    request failed", which is indistinguishable from a real connectivity
    problem and sends you debugging the wrong layer entirely.
  - The Authorization header, read from the live Supabase session rather
    than a passed-in token, so a caller cannot send a stale one.
  - The error envelope. This fixes a live bug: create-profile.tsx read
    `errorData.error`, a field the API has never sent -- its shape is
    { statusCode, message, timestamp, path, method }. So every validation
    failure showed the generic "Failed to create profile" and threw away
    the per-field messages saying exactly what was wrong. ApiError.messages
    is now always an array whether the server sent a string or an array,
    and describeApiError() also handles non-JSON 5xx bodies, which starts
    mattering the moment this sits behind an ALB.

types/types.ts becomes types/{coach,conversation,reference,user,workout}.ts
behind a barrel at @/types. One 139-line file holding every view type meant
a guaranteed merge conflict on every slice. Same reasoning as landing the
client alone. Profile / Federation / Division / WeightClass move here out
of create-profile.tsx.

Splitting them surfaced two wrong types, which only typechecked because
Supabase's `data` is untyped:

  - Federation.id, Division.id and WeightClass.id were `number`. They are
    uuids, so strings.
  - WeightClass.sort_order was `boolean`. It is a smallint.

Correcting nullability then made strict mode reject two call sites where
the UI assumed reference-data `name` was always present. It is nullable in
the schema, so both now have a fallback -- federation falls back to `code`,
which is NOT NULL.

Verified: frontend lint and type-check both clean, tailwind compiles with
no dead classes. The @/types barrel uses the same directory-index pattern
as the existing @/components/ui, so Metro resolves it the same way.

arms would be dead code and `/check` would 500 over an outage again. **0.6.3** is the same shape moved
onto an argument — `load_dotenv_file` had reached none of the six cache resolvers, so the `False` we

and check the flags you already pass as well as the symbols you already import: upgrading all three in
step here would have been wrong, and so would treating an enricher patch as beneath reading.

**And having read one, be willing to say it is not load-bearing. `0.6.4` is the first enricher floor
here that is *not* hard** — one fix in upstream's ClinVar drafter, no public symbol moved, nothing this
service runs behaving differently, and a deployment left on 0.6.3 is not broken. It is the floor
because the lock had already resolved it and the release's suite ran on that trio, so leaving the floor
behind would permit an assembly nobody tested. Record which kind a floor is when you add one: the
0.6.2 and 0.6.3 comments run long because both were easy to mistake for optional, and that whole
argument is wasted if a later reader learns to skim every floor as mandatory.

**A version-gap check belongs to the thing that has versions.** Most of 0.6.3 is upstream's ClinVar and
ClinPGx *drafters*, and the honest answer for this service was that it has none — drafting is
authoring-side, so "modules published before this need a re-draft" is a message for module authors and
not a `registry upgrade` sweep. Nothing recompiles here: the compiler stayed at 0.6.1, and a compiler
patch is deliberately not a gap. Say that in the release rather than leaving a reader to infer it, or
the next operator runs the UPGRADE.md sweep expecting it to fix a drafted module, and it cannot.

**The other half of that: advice forwarded on somebody else's behalf is still ours to correct.** 0.18.1
passed upstream's remediation along as *those modules need a fresh upload from their publisher*, and
0.6.4 (S45) is upstream measuring what 0.6.3 had not — a re-draft of the existing spec **appends** the
corrected rows beside the ones they supersede, so the shorter instruction produces a module worse-formed
than either the old one or a new one. The publisher needs a fresh spec directory. Two things generalise.
A remediation we relay is a claim we made, so re-read it when its source is re-measured. And **before
building a detector for a defect like this, ask whether the artifact can even carry the evidence** — the
superseded rows are invisible from inside a published module (coordinate rows carry no `rsid`; the
obvious predicate finds 0 of 31), so a facet or `revalidate` rule would report clean on every affected
module, which is worse than having none.

FOUND AND FIXED (real, verified bugs):

1. AdminDeviceModelRepository::delete() — queried products.device_model_id,
   a column Phase 1 dropped (device_model_product is the sole compatibility
   source of truth since then). Every admin attempt to delete ANY device
   model — even one with zero linked products — threw a SQL 500
   ("no such column: device_model_id"). Completely untested path. Fixed
   by dropping the dead column check; the device_model_product pivot
   check (already correct) is now the only guard.

2. DeviceEnforcementService::assertModelsSelectable() N+1 — called up to
   500 times per request from BulkProductService::createProducts() (once
   per Excel row), re-querying the same device model/category chain every
   time even when rows repeat the same model/category (the common case).
   Added a request-scoped instance cache (model chain + category family
   ids) — same public signature, same error messages, zero cross-request
   leakage (service is resolved fresh per request).

3. BulkProductService::createProducts() N+1 — resolved category/brand/
   device-model by slug with a separate query per row (validateFile()
   already had this exact problem fixed with whereIn batching; createProducts()
   did not). Measured before/after: 5 rows / 20 rows went from 60 / 240
   queries (12/row, purely linear) to 28 / 83 queries — the batchable part
   no longer grows with row count; only the inherent per-row insert/
   uniqueness-check/sync cost remains.

    if not request.user.is_authenticated:
        raise PermissionDenied('Authentication required')

        Return True if the user has the specified permission. Query all
        available auth backends, but return immediately if any backend returns
        True. Thus, a user who has permission from a single auth backend is
        assumed to have permission in general. If an object is provided, check
        permissions for that object.

        if self.is_active and self.is_superuser:

        # Otherwise we need to check the backends.

explanation:
Fixed API token authentication bypassed when path contains `/healthz`

The APITokenAuthMiddleware allowed bypassing the check if the path included `/healthz`. An attacker only needed to include `/healthz` in the URL, even the querystring, to bypass the API token check, for example `/v1.0/invoke/myapp/method/something?foo=/healthz`.

Additionally, this was not checking the method of the request, so requests to `POST /healthz` would cause a service invocation to happen.

This fixes the issue by making the check a lot more strict. The API token check can be bypassed only if:

- The path is exactly `/v1.0/healthz` or `/v1.0/healthz/outbound` (slashes are trimmed on each side)
- The method is `GET`

Authentication Bypass For Endpoints With Anonymous Access

Using a remember-me cookie with an arbitrary username can cause Opencast
to assume proper authentication for that user even if the remember-me
cookie was incorrect given that the attacked endpoint also allows
anonymous access.

This way, an attacker can, for example, fake a remember-me token, assume
the identity of the global system administrator and request non-public
content from the search service without ever providing any proper
authentication.

The reason for this problem is that using a remember-me cookie will
always cause the user in the request context to be populated, even if
the cookie is invalid by now. This is usually no problem, except in
combination with anonymous access where anonymous authentication is
granted and the request may continue.

In such a case, Opencast's security service would just check that a user
existed in the request context and assume proper authentication of this
user, never checking if it's actually anonymous authentication.

This patch adds this additional check, falling back to the anonymous
user in case of anonymous authentication.

explanation:
Fix real vulnerabilities found in a dedicated security audit

Three parallel audits (auth/authz, injection/input-handling, secrets/
infrastructure) covering the whole app, adversarial lens. Fixes:

CRITICAL
- MFA was completely bypassable: the 5-minute "mfa_pending" challenge
  token issued by /auth/login (before a TOTP/backup code is ever
  checked) decoded and passed get_current_user()'s checks exactly like
  a real session token -- anyone with just a password (the one thing
  MFA exists to add a second factor against) could call any
  authenticated endpoint directly with it, no code required, for the
  full 5-minute window. Now explicitly rejected, same pattern as the
  existing "purpose" claim check.

HIGH
- Twilio webhook signature verification failed OPEN (skipped, request
  allowed through) when TWILIO_TOKEN/PUBLIC_BASE_URL were unset --
  now fails closed (503), matching the pattern already used correctly
  for CRON_SECRET/EMAIL_WORKER_SECRET.
- SECRET_KEY/JWT_SECRET ship with hardcoded, publicly-known placeholder
  defaults with no code-level guard against running with them in
  production (only Render's generateValue: true prevented this on the
  documented deploy path). App now refuses to boot with DEBUG=false if
  either is still its literal default.

MODERATE
- Three IDOR gaps: POST /communications/send's maintenance_update
  template, POST /maintenance/'s unit_id/tenant_id, and POST
  /accounting/expenses' vendor_id all accepted a foreign org's UUID
  with no ownership check, leaking that resource's name/title/status
  back in the response. All now validated against the caller's org.
- Unescaped HTML injection in three outreach-email templates
  (services/lead_service.py) -- lead fields (scraped from public,
  attacker-editable Google Business Profile data, or typed into
  POST /leads with no sanitization) were interpolated into HTML emails
  with no output encoding. Now html.escape()'d for the HTML body
  specifically (plain-text body unaffected).
- SSRF in the lead-scraper's email-discovery fetch
  (workers/tasks/lead_scraping.py) -- a Places listing's self-reported
  website URL was fetched with no scheme/private-IP allowlist and
  followed redirects blindly, so a listing pointed at an internal
  address or a cloud metadata endpoint would have the server fetch it.
  Added an SSRF guard checked on the initial URL and re-checked on
  every redirect hop.
- FastAPI backend sent no security headers at all (X-Frame-Options,
  X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) --
  only the Next.js frontend did, despite security.tsx's copy claiming
  this applies to "every response." Left /docs and /redoc unprotected
  against framing. Added a headers middleware.
- ALLOWED_ORIGINS="*" combined with allow_credentials=True (a plausible
  operator typo in Render's env vars) would silently make CORS reflect
  any origin with credentials -- app now refuses to boot with that
  combination instead.
- Three endpoints doing real, billed AI/scraping work (inspection photo
  AI analysis, the Claude marketing-copy generator, the lead-scrape
  trigger) had zero rate limiting or cost cap beyond role/plan gating --
  a compromised privileged account or a buggy retry loop had no
  built-in ceiling on Anthropic/OpenAI/Google Places billing, and on
  this single-worker server a burst could also stall every other
  tenant's requests. Added reasonable per-minute limits to all three.

Not fixed here, flagged for a follow-up decision (both require either
a schema migration or a product/UX tradeoff, not a mechanical fix):
- Password reset tokens (staff-side /auth/reset-password) are replayable
  within their 30-minute window -- not marked single-use like the
  tenant-portal equivalent already is.
- Rate limiting on login/reset/2FA is per-IP only, no per-account
  lockout/backoff -- a distributed credential-stuffing attempt across
  many source IPs isn't meaningfully throttled today.
- API keys are stored and compared in plaintext (high-entropy,
  infeasible to brute-force, but a DB-level compromise would expose
  live keys directly rather than hashes) -- hashing at rest would need
  a rotation flow since existing keys can't be un-hashed.

`agentActions.chipAuthLevel.test.js` (new), `AIAgent.chips.test.js` (updated).

**What was broken:** the whole action region sat behind `{isLoggedIn &&
renderActionGroups()}` inside an `isLoggedIn ? … : …` ternary, so a guest saw a
login prompt INSTEAD of the action surface. That violates the product rule —
*show all actions, then authenticate when the use case requires it, and we have
SoT* — in two ways: it removed the demo's discovery story, and it invented a
second source of truth (a bare `isLoggedIn` at a render site) alongside the
`uc.auth` SoT the rest of the app gates on.

**What was fixed:** discovery is ungated — `renderActionGroups()` now renders
for everyone. The auth challenge moved to DISPATCH: `handleChipActivate` reads
the chip's declared level via `chipAuthLevel()` and, when the viewer does not
meet it, offers sign-in (`showLoginPromptAction`, same shape
`handleDemoStepSelect` uses) instead of dispatching. Chip levels are declared in
`agentActions.js` because chips are not use cases and carry no server `uc.auth`.

**Do not break:** `chipAuthLevel` is **FAIL-CLOSED** — anything not in
`PUBLIC_CHIP_IDS` needs a session, and a blank/missing id resolves to `user`,
never `public`. Only add an id to `PUBLIC_CHIP_IDS` when the action genuinely
works with no user context; getting it wrong shows a guest a chip that 401s
instead of prompting. `mcp_tools` is public deliberately (its endpoint carries
no auth middleware and answers 200 anonymously) — it sits in the `admin` GROUP
for menu placement only, and **UI grouping is not an authorization boundary**.
`logout` stays exempt (it IS the session action). Ungating the render WITHOUT
the dispatch gate would be a regression, not a fix.

offers sign-in rather than dispatching.
