def _get_store() -> rag.VectorStore:
    global _store
    if _store is None:
        _store = rag.VectorStore.load()
    return _store

def handle(message: str, trace: Trace) -> str:
    hits = _get_store().search(message, k=3)
    relevant = [h for h in hits if h.score >= rag.RELEVANCE_FLOOR]

    if not relevant:
        # Grounding guarantee: no relevant doc -> abstain, don't invent.
        raise AbstainError("no knowledge-base match above relevance floor")

    context = "\n\n".join(f"[{h.doc.source}] {h.doc.text}" for h in relevant)

Repoints Eloquent from local MySQL to Supabase Postgres (the actual
production database), then fixes the real bugs that surfaced once the
app was actually exercised end-to-end against it:

- Locks down anon-role database access: every table had unrestricted
  read/write/delete via the exposed Supabase anon key, including the
  users table (password hashes). Revoked access to internal tables and
  restricted app tables to the exact operations the frontend uses.

  registration fail with a not-null violation.
- Removes a dead `section` text column on users that shadowed the
  section() relationship, silently breaking teacher approval of
  students (always evaluated to null, so ownership checks always
  failed).
- Fixes real IDOR: a teacher could approve/reject/reset any student
  platform-wide, not just their own section's.
- Stops leaking the AI API key to the browser; proxies quiz generation
  through the server instead.
- Rebuilds teacher/admin/student analytics from real Supabase data
  instead of hardcoded zeros, rand(), and a disconnected admin_users
  table that was never actually used by auth.
- Fixes silent quiz-publish duplication (missing unique constraint
  meant "replace" actually inserted a duplicate row).
- Adds unclosed-<script> and broken-relationship fixes found via live
  browser testing, plus 30+ new feature tests covering the above.

The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {

Unauth callers ate a wasted bookingRequests SELECT before hitting a

because it's a 403→401 client-behavior change; on inspection the reprice
client is always an authenticated logged-in customer, so a 401 only fires
for callers that shouldn't be reaching the endpoint at all.

1. Explicit 401 at the door — before the DB fetch — with an honest

Both branches unchanged behaviorally for legitimate callers.

None. Completes the auth-slippage sweep on booking-requests.ts —
prior sweep PRs #1904 (confirm), #1911 (7 POSTs), #1912 (GET). This
covers the last remaining router-mounted handler with the same shape.

## Risk
Very low. 401 replaces 403 for anon callers only (a case that already
denied). Legitimate customer + admin repricing unchanged.

Per standing CEO directive.

Auth Phase B final-review fix wave: per-league authz + 11 follow-ups

Closes the findings from the final whole-branch review of Auth Phase B.

Critical -- per-league authorization. Any signed-in user could read any
other user's connected league via /league/{their-league-id}. Adds
ownsLeague() (web/lib/leagueConnection.ts) and enforces it at the two
web-layer choke points all browser traffic funnels through: the shared
/league/[leagueId] layout (redirect to "/", reusing app/page.tsx's
existing routing) and all 3 /api/league/[leagueId]/* Route Handlers (401
signed out, 403 not the owner). Deliberately not applied to the sim API's
12 pre-existing /league/{league_id}/* routes -- that service binds to
127.0.0.1:8123 and is reachable only by the Next.js server, so the web
layer is the real perimeter.

Important:
- reingest: broaden per-user error isolation to a _SKIPPABLE_ERRORS tuple
  (EspnFetchError, CredentialEncryptionError, IngestError), mirroring
  sim/api/precompute.py, so a rotated encryption key or one malformed
  payload no longer aborts the whole batch.
- reingest: re-resolve the season on every run and write back the season
  ingest_league actually parsed, instead of re-using the connect-time
  value forever and re-fetching last season after a rollover.
- scheduler: anchor the two interval triggers apart so re-ingest always
  runs first and precompute follows 15 minutes behind, every cycle. Note
  IntervalTrigger only honors a future start_date -- one already in the
  past is rounded forward a whole interval -- hence
  REINGEST_STARTUP_LEAD_SECONDS; this is also why neither job ever
  actually ran "once immediately" as the old docstring claimed.
- Strengthen the credential-leak HTTP test to submit a distinctive fake
  espn_s2 and assert it appears in neither the response body nor caplog.
- decisions.md: correct the Phase 17 entry's two overclaims (live ESPN
  verification is pending the owner, not performed) and record this wave.
- Remove the last stale DEFAULT_LEAGUE_ID references.

Minor: catch CredentialEncryptionError in connect_league_route (500,
mirroring AnalystConfigError); espn_s2/SWID inputs are type="password"
with autofill and spellcheck off; two `assert row is not None` narrowings
become explicit raises (asserts are stripped under python -O); rename the
shadowed local `body` in authedFetch to responseBody.

Also wires espn_team_id into its first real consumer: the connected
user's own team is now the default selection on Beat My League (the one
page labeled "Choose your team", and whose docstring cited the missing
logged-in identity). An explicit ?team= still wins.

at the pre-existing baseline, confirmed identical by re-running on clean
main; tsc, eslint, and next build clean in /web; scheduler ordering
manually verified.

1.9.3 - `unreleased`

- Fixed arbitrary certificate revocation at the CA (`GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67`_). Certificate identity was tracked
  only by Lemur's internal database row, not by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated principal could
  upload a duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing ``authority_id`` and
  ``serial``) and then revoke it via ``PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke``, causing the CA to revoke the
  real certificate belonging to another principal. ``POST /api/1/certificates/upload`` now requires
  ``AuthorityPermission`` on the specified authority, and rejects uploads whose ``(authority_id, serial)``
  pair already matches an existing certificate with a ``409`` response. ``PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke``
  now also checks authorization and endpoint attachment against every certificate row sharing
  ``(authority_id, serial)`` with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request, closing the
  gap for any duplicate rows that already exist.

**Root Cause**:
Permission configuration updates trigger MCP service restarts. The previous implementation was starting the agent loop immediately after initiating permission updates, causing conflicts when the MCP service was still restarting.

2. **MCP service readiness check**: Wait for MCP service to fully restart before proceeding
3. **Verification logging**: Add detailed logs to track permission verification and service status

- Modified `handlePermissionResponse` to wait for permission config completion
- Added `waitForMcpServiceReady` method to ensure MCP service is ready
- Enhanced verification logging to track server permissions and service status
- Proper timing: Permission grant → MCP restart → Service ready → Agent loop restart

This ensures that when the agent loop restarts, all permissions are properly configured and MCP services are fully operational, preventing tool call failures due to timing issues.

## Broken leg
The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Not authorized to reprice this booking' });
    }

Unauth callers ate a wasted bookingRequests SELECT before hitting a
MISLEADING 403 that suggested a permissions problem, not a
credentials problem. The audit agent classified this as "risky-cosmetic"
because it's a 403→401 client-behavior change; on inspection the reprice
client is always an authenticated logged-in customer, so a 401 only fires
for callers that shouldn't be reaching the endpoint at all.

## Fix (server-only, split into two clean checks)
1. Explicit 401 at the door — before the DB fetch — with an honest
   'Authentication required' message.
2. Ownership check no longer needs the !userId branch — reads cleanly
   as "owner OR verified admin".

Both branches unchanged behaviorally for legitimate callers.

server/tests/reprice-401-hygiene.regression.test.ts — 3 pins:
  ✓ returns 401 explicitly when there is no userId

None. Completes the auth-slippage sweep on booking-requests.ts —
prior sweep PRs #1904 (confirm), #1911 (7 POSTs), #1912 (GET). This
covers the last remaining router-mounted handler with the same shape.

## Risk
Very low. 401 replaces 403 for anon callers only (a case that already
denied). Legitimate customer + admin repricing unchanged.

Per standing CEO directive.

Harden human review and blind freeze governance (#17)

* test(freeze): cover the one-way human blind-v3 freeze contract

freeze_human_blind_v3.py had no test importing it at all, despite being
the only irreversible step on the path out of QUALIFIED_SHADOW: it
hashes a selected human-adjudicated set and commits those samples to
FROZEN. Every comparable path in the repository — backup rotation,
release audit, migration restore, light verification — already has a
contract test.

The fixture builds an adjudicated corpus sitting exactly at the
production minimums (30 RISK_REVIEW / 30 NON_TARGET / 20 ABSTAIN across
four source families, one distinct issuer, chain, passage and text hash
per event). Sitting at the minimum is deliberate: excluding a single
event must then break the freeze, which is what proves --exclude-jsonl
reaches the selector instead of being read and discarded.

Pinned invariants:
- a candidate build writes the dataset and manifest but leaves every
  sample READY, carries no rows inside the manifest, and reports zero
  entity, chain, exact-text and near-duplicate overlap
- the same corpus yields the same freeze id and the same dataset bytes
- artifacts are written atomically, owner-only, leaving no .tmp behind
- --apply refuses an absent authorization id, actor, expiry, or a
  purpose under twenty characters, and refuses an expired one
- every refusal leaves all samples unfrozen and writes no manifest, so
  no artifact can later be mistaken for an authorized freeze receipt
- an authorized apply freezes exactly the selected samples under the
  manifest freeze id, records the authorization, and reports the model
  and canonical ledger as unchanged
- a second authorized run cannot re-freeze or re-identify the set
- the exclusion loader normalizes hash case, skips blank lines, rejects
  a non-object row, and collects all seven overlap dimensions

Each guard was mutation-checked: removing the authorization test, the
expiry test, the missing-reference test, the exclusion wiring, or the
freeze call itself turns the corresponding tests red.

Coverage of the script goes from 0% to 99%; suite is 719 passed with 21
subtests.

One observation left unpinned for review: the dataset file is written
before the --apply authorization check, so a refused commit can leave a
dataset with no manifest beside it. The tests assert the safety
invariants (nothing frozen, no manifest) without fixing that ordering
in place, so reordering it later stays a deliberate choice.

explanation:
Fix real vulnerabilities found in a dedicated security audit

Three parallel audits (auth/authz, injection/input-handling, secrets/
infrastructure) covering the whole app, adversarial lens. Fixes:

CRITICAL
- MFA was completely bypassable: the 5-minute "mfa_pending" challenge
  token issued by /auth/login (before a TOTP/backup code is ever
  checked) decoded and passed get_current_user()'s checks exactly like
  a real session token -- anyone with just a password (the one thing
  MFA exists to add a second factor against) could call any
  authenticated endpoint directly with it, no code required, for the
  full 5-minute window. Now explicitly rejected, same pattern as the
  existing "purpose" claim check.

HIGH
- Twilio webhook signature verification failed OPEN (skipped, request
  allowed through) when TWILIO_TOKEN/PUBLIC_BASE_URL were unset --
  now fails closed (503), matching the pattern already used correctly
  for CRON_SECRET/EMAIL_WORKER_SECRET.
- SECRET_KEY/JWT_SECRET ship with hardcoded, publicly-known placeholder
  defaults with no code-level guard against running with them in
  production (only Render's generateValue: true prevented this on the
  documented deploy path). App now refuses to boot with DEBUG=false if
  either is still its literal default.

MODERATE
- Three IDOR gaps: POST /communications/send's maintenance_update
  template, POST /maintenance/'s unit_id/tenant_id, and POST
  /accounting/expenses' vendor_id all accepted a foreign org's UUID
  with no ownership check, leaking that resource's name/title/status
  back in the response. All now validated against the caller's org.
- Unescaped HTML injection in three outreach-email templates
  (services/lead_service.py) -- lead fields (scraped from public,
  attacker-editable Google Business Profile data, or typed into
  POST /leads with no sanitization) were interpolated into HTML emails
  with no output encoding. Now html.escape()'d for the HTML body
  specifically (plain-text body unaffected).
- SSRF in the lead-scraper's email-discovery fetch
  (workers/tasks/lead_scraping.py) -- a Places listing's self-reported
  website URL was fetched with no scheme/private-IP allowlist and
  followed redirects blindly, so a listing pointed at an internal
  address or a cloud metadata endpoint would have the server fetch it.
  Added an SSRF guard checked on the initial URL and re-checked on
  every redirect hop.
- FastAPI backend sent no security headers at all (X-Frame-Options,
  X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) --
  only the Next.js frontend did, despite security.tsx's copy claiming
  this applies to "every response." Left /docs and /redoc unprotected
  against framing. Added a headers middleware.
- ALLOWED_ORIGINS="*" combined with allow_credentials=True (a plausible
  operator typo in Render's env vars) would silently make CORS reflect
  any origin with credentials -- app now refuses to boot with that
  combination instead.
- Three endpoints doing real, billed AI/scraping work (inspection photo
  AI analysis, the Claude marketing-copy generator, the lead-scrape
  trigger) had zero rate limiting or cost cap beyond role/plan gating --
  a compromised privileged account or a buggy retry loop had no
  built-in ceiling on Anthropic/OpenAI/Google Places billing, and on
  this single-worker server a burst could also stall every other
  tenant's requests. Added reasonable per-minute limits to all three.

Not fixed here, flagged for a follow-up decision (both require either
a schema migration or a product/UX tradeoff, not a mechanical fix):
- Password reset tokens (staff-side /auth/reset-password) are replayable
  within their 30-minute window -- not marked single-use like the
  tenant-portal equivalent already is.
- Rate limiting on login/reset/2FA is per-IP only, no per-account
  lockout/backoff -- a distributed credential-stuffing attempt across
  many source IPs isn't meaningfully throttled today.
- API keys are stored and compared in plaintext (high-entropy,
  infeasible to brute-force, but a DB-level compromise would expose
  live keys directly rather than hashes) -- hashing at rest would need
  a rotation flow since existing keys can't be un-hashed.

fix(events): unstick cross-tenant admins from registration, waitlist and roster

Closes the corner 766b867d2 deliberately left open. Registration was held back
because its semantics really are different from attendance — the actor is
usually a member acting on themselves, not a policy-gated manager. Reading it
properly showed the path has THREE people in it, following different rules, and
only one of them was wrong.

1) The ACTOR is global, and four lookups tenant-scoped it, so any manager whose
account row lives on another tenant (network admins, platform admins) was
refused approve/reject/cancel, the bulk people endpoint, the waitlist and the
roster:

- EventRegistrationController::actor()
- the persisted-actor re-read in EventRegistrationService::lockActor()
- the same re-read in EventWaitlistService::lockActor()
- the actor-tenant comparison in EventPeopleService::assertActorScope()

Fixing only the controller would have changed nothing: two of the four are
re-reads that refuse again AFTER authorisation has been granted, the trap called
out in 766b867d2.

Root Cause: the acting user's own identity lookup was tenant-scoped. Auth is
global in this codebase; only resources are tenant-scoped.

Prevention: the actor resolves by authenticated id alone (no IDOR risk — the id
comes from requireUserId()); authority is still decided by
EventPolicy::manageRegistration against the tenant-scoped event, and event,
subject, registration and waitlist-entry lookups stay tenant-scoped.

2) The SUBJECT stays same-tenant, and that is now documented rather than
looking like the bug. EventsController::legacyRegistrationActor() keeps its
tenant predicate: all four of its call sites pass the authenticated id as BOTH
actor and subject (self-service RSVP / waitlist), and a participation subject
must belong to the event's tenant — EventParticipationEligibilityService,
"the boundary for every writer", enforces exactly that
(event_participation_scope_invalid) and then runs safeguarding contact checks
that are tenant-local by construction. Dropping the predicate would have changed
no outcome; the subject lookup in lockParticipants() refuses the same caller a
moment later. A comment at the lookup records this, and
EventRegistrationController now splits actor() (global, management) from
selfActor() (same-tenant, self-service) so the rule is visible in code. The
split also keeps a cross-tenant member's refusal a truthful 403 rather than the
404 "member not found" the subject lookup would raise deeper in the stack.

3) NOT FIXED, and pinned by a test that says so:
EventParticipationEligibilityService resolves the event's ORGANIZER with
AND tenant_id = ? before the safeguarding checks, so an event created by a
cross-tenant organiser accepts no registrations at all — including a local
member registering themselves. 5373940c8 made that event creatable and
publishable, so it is reachable. It is left alone because the fix is not simply
dropping the predicate: SafeguardingInteractionPolicy exposes
assertCrossTenantContactAllowed() as a distinct evaluation from
assertLocalContactAllowed(), so resolving the organizer globally while still
calling the local check would skip a safeguarding boundary rather than honour
it. That is an owner decision, and
test_event_owned_by_a_cross_tenant_organizer_still_refuses_registration will
fail the moment it changes.

Verified: 10 new tests in EventRegistrationCrossTenantActorTest green, 7 of them
confirmed to fail against the old code with the bug's own reason codes
(event_registration_actor_invalid, event_waitlist_actor_not_found,
event_registration_authorization_denied). 60 tests green across the
registration, waitlist, people and legacy-parity suites. PHPStan clean on all
five changed files. The whole Feature/Events + EventsControllerTest run produces
a failure set byte-identical to the same run against reverted code, so this
change introduces no new failures — but note that set is not empty: 9 tests in
EventPolicyTest, EventOutboxFoundationTest and EventHealthCommandTest fail in
isolation on already-pushed main and need separate attention.

feat: add the behavioural eval tier and its gates

Does the agent use MCTS when it should, use it properly, and does it work. This adds the
behavioural eval tier: scorers with denominators, the gates that keep them honest, a
vitest-evals runner against Workers AI, and the first two live run records.

MAKING THE ROOT SUITES RUNNABLE. The four root e2e suites were skipped and therefore proved
nothing. Two independent omissions kept them dead. They gated on PROTEUS_AUTH, an AI Gateway
token, which is the one credential this account does not need: the default model is native
Workers AI DeepSeek, and a deployed worker already fronts it at /api/user/ai/v1 for any CLI
bearer. And the root `tests/` directory was typechecked by NOTHING: `bun run check` named
eight projects and not one included it.

Pointed at the project compiler for the first time, `tests/` produced 23 errors, calls to
APIs deleted months ago. The worst is `BuiltinToolDeps.engine`, passed at 9 call sites and
silently ignored at runtime, so every one of these suites built its toolset with evolution
NOT WIRED and then asserted on evolution events. Also `EvolutionEngine.onTurnComplete` (now
`reviewTurn`), `EvolutionConfig.sessionReflectionInterval`/`turnCraftThreshold`,
`SessionWriter.compact`, `WorkspaceInfo.id`, and `generateText({maxSteps})`. Setting a token
on the tree as it stood would have produced a red suite, not evidence. A permanently-skipped
test is not merely unproven, it decays, and the decay is invisible until someone tries to run
it.

- `resolveLiveModel` resolves a target from PROTEUS_ORIGIN + PROTEUS_TOKEN (the worker proxy,
  native Workers AI) or AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL + AI_GATEWAY_AUTH. A HALF-set environment returns
  `misconfigured` and THROWS: partial config used to resolve to an empty auth header and a
  silent skip.
- No hardcoded gateway URL. The four suites each carried the same account id in a fallback
  default; a public repo should not, and a harness that silently falls back cannot state which
  target it measured.
- One `liveChatModel` via core's `createChatModel`, so live runs inherit `withRateLimitRetry`.
  The four hand-rolled providers did not, making a mid-run 429 read as a behavioural failure.
- `recordLiveModelSpend`/`reportLiveModelSpend` measure what a run cost. Cost per run is not a
  constant when the model may take 500 steps.
- All 23 type errors repaired against current APIs with no assertion weakened. The single
  removed `expect` is `info.id`, whose invariant the adjacent
  `expect(rt2.identity.id).toBe(agentId)` already asserts.
- `tests/tsconfig.json`, wired into `bun run check`. The tsconfig is not the fix; `check`
  running it is.

Counts unchanged: 3 pass, 19 skip, 0 fail, 26 expect() calls.

THE RICH SCORERS. Three scorers, each reading through the PRODUCTION reader and each
reporting how many eligible things it looked at, separately from how many passed.

- `scoreExploration`: competed runs, of those how many opened more than ONE branch, how many
  the reader can hand a winning score for, and how many had that ranking survive into the
  store as exactly one terminal node. A run can return a `winnerId` in memory while no row was
  ever marked: ranked to the caller, unranked to every later reader.
- `scoreSettleVisibility`: for each settle mode's write store, does `listForkRuns` (what the
  Exploration pane calls) return what was written. Asks the reader for more rows than were
  written, because it slices AFTER merging its two halves, so its own window must never look
  like a missing row.
- `scoreDelegation`: per-arm {eligible, converted, rate} over `turn_steering`, never pooled:
  the step-25 arm only fires on turns the turn-start arm did not convert. `rate` is null for
  an empty arm, not 0; a rate over no turns is absent, not zero.

Two false zeros were caught inside the harness itself before it shipped. `scoreDelegation`
was first written against `tool_call_start` rows naming the `agents` tool. NO production code
emits that event type on either backend, the sinks emit `tool_call_end` and `step_finish`, so
it would have reported "never delegated" forever, on every run, and been believed. It now
counts `head_split`, which is what a fork actually writes, and a regression test pins the
shape. `alternate_takes` also has no `root_id` column, so the take lookup joins back through
`search_nodes`; a `WHERE root_id = …` would have matched nothing.

Every scorer has an empty-store test asserting a ZERO denominator rather than a pass, and
`scoreSettleVisibility` takes its reader as a seam so its negative controls can hand it the
reader AS IT WAS when the bug shipped, one that reads a single half, in both directions.
Today's reader returns any root in either store, so without that the green result would be
indistinguishable from a scorer that never looks. 18 tests, credential-free.

The live evals (tests/evals/) assert those scores against a real target: exploration drives
the fork through the real `agents` tool so the model cannot decline, and delegation drives
three FRESH workspaces through the full LocalAgentSession turn spine, because the turn-start
predicate needs a fresh ask, so N turns in one session would give a denominator of 1 while
looking like N. Its prompts are imperatives because the predicate refuses anything ending in
? or !. The denominator is asserted exactly; the RATE is reported, not gated, because at this
sample size a floor is a coin flip dressed as a gate.

THE EIGHT-SCORER PANEL. The reward signal CL-Bench found missing. Its first run recorded 14
evolution events in 14 turns, every one "ungraded (no follow-up) | 0 tool calls", ending at
scaffoldVersion 0 / craftedToolCount 0: evolution fired with nothing to learn from. These are
the instruments that grade a turn.

A uniform BehaviourScorer panel sits beside the three rich scorers, reading what the harness
already records: steering conversion across all five triggers, the craft loop closing
(crafted → reused), edits landing, recovery findings that HELD, completion honesty, spill
retrieval, and tool outcomes. Every one carries an explicit denominator and reports rate=null,
never 0, when nothing was eligible, because 0/0 is a fact about the task and 0/7 is a fact
about the agent.

Three of these needed their obvious form rejected:

  - recovery_durability over recoveries is a tautology: the event exists only when a streak
    was already broken, so n/n = 1.00 forever. Scored instead over the producer's own named
    falsifier, a signature recovered twice necessarily failed again.
  - completion_honesty inverts polarity. converted=true means the gate caught a premature
    completion claim, so the numerator is the UN-converted rows. Scored the obvious way round
    it would reward declaring victory early.
  - spill_retrieval excludes spills with no resolvable address. There was nothing to read
    back, so charging it to the agent scores our defect.

Exports parseStoredRunEvent, the canonical parse RunEventRecorder already uses, and reads
through it, which deleted seven local interfaces copying shapes the producer owns. Type
narrowing is in SQL, unlike the recorder's own reader, so one malformed row costs one number
instead of all eight. That switch also caught the fixture: it wrote only type-specific fields
while production persists the whole stamped event, so every json_extract scorer read it
happily while the canonical parse rejected it, the write/read disagreement this module's
docstring warns about, inside its own tests.

41/41 green. Each scorer has a pass, a RED on the defect it exists for, and a
zero-denominator case; a trigger outside the producer's picklist is pinned to throw rather
than quietly leave the denominator.

THE GATES. Two gates for the same defect class, both found by trying to run tests nobody had
run: a signal that is missing is indistinguishable from a signal that is fine, unless
something asserts the corpus was non-empty.

`gate:skip-ratchet` locks the SET of skipped tests, with a written reason per entry.
`bun test ./tests/` reports 23 skips and exits 0, and the exit code is all anyone reads.
Locking the set rather than a count is the point: a count of 23 cannot tell you a different 23
are skipping now. It also fails when a locked skip starts running, so the ratchet only
tightens; and it asserts every target contributed a test, because `bun test tests` and
`bun test tests/` both match NOTHING here and only `./tests/` selects them. `--lock`
deliberately refuses to write: a reason is not something a script can generate.

`gate:typecheck-coverage` derives the project list from the `check` script, following
`bun run` transitively, without which it demands an exclusion for `tools/oxlint/anti-slop`,
which IS covered, and compares it against every directory on disk holding a `*.test.ts`. The
root `tests/` directory was covered by nothing, which is how four suites came to call two
deleted APIs. Both sides must be non-empty or `assertMeasured` kills the run.

Both gates have their own tests, 23 of them, including the one that matters most: a JUnit
parse matching only self-closing `<testcase/>` elements reports every SKIPPED test as absent,
so the ratchet would reconcile an empty set and pass forever.

`test:eval` is the tier. It names the target and cost basis BEFORE spending anything, runs the
suites once, enforces the ratchet over THAT report rather than a second run, and prints the
measured spend. With no credentials it still runs and still passes, because a tier nobody can
reproduce without a secret is not a tier, while the ratchet stays mandatory. Targets are
root-relative because `bun test --cwd` does not read the root bunfig.toml and silently loses
both the throwaway PROTEUS_HOME and pathIgnorePatterns. Cost is reported as measured model
calls and tokens, never dollars: a price is a platform number and the catalog carries limits,
not prices.

Wired into LADDER (commit / push / ci) and deploy.sh, keeping the two in the same order;
deploy.test.ts asserts exact equality. The existing ci `bun test ./tests/` entry keeps its
place but its text was wrong on all three counts it claimed (22 tests, 19 skips,
PROTEUS_AUTH); its `blind` now names what it cannot see, a suite whose code no longer
compiles, because bun strips types.

DEPENDENCIES. package.json resolves to main's side, strictly newer on both blocks:
root-relative `bun test packages/*/` over the old `--cwd` spelling, plus test:workerd, the
cf-backend/tests/workerd typecheck project and the no-ambient-git gate. vitest-evals is pinned
exactly. 0.x with 30 releases and two root-API reshapes already: the scorer-first
`describeEval({data, task, scorers})` moved to `vitest-evals/legacy` at 0.9.0, so a caret
range would silently change API. Peer is vitest >=4 <5 and we are on 4.1.10, which
pool-workers 0.21.3 also peers, so one vitest serves both pools.

MODELS, verified against the account's own catalogue rather than derived from each other; the
suffixes differ and a guess would have been wrong:

  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $PROTEUS_TOKEN" $PROTEUS_ORIGIN/api/user/ai/v1/models
    pro    @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-pro-0813    (= DEFAULT_WORKERS_AI_MODEL_ID)
    flash  @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731  (exposed and serving)

Both answered real completions. A two-point measurement at fixed prompt puts pro at exactly
3.0x flash per token on both coefficients, which turns "flash for volume, pro for bounds" into
a budget; a run record declares which regime made it.

WHAT MAKES A RUN EVIDENCE. `assessAdmissibility` refuses to call a run a measurement without
graded turns, tool calls, at least one scorer with a non-zero denominator, and an executed
task set equal to the declared one. The last is the measured-set/governed-set equality as an
assertion; the first two are what CL-Bench lacked when it reported mean_gain -0.2 over a
corpus whose every turn was "ungraded | 0 tool calls" with 500 steps available and one used.

WHY THE HARNESS THROWS, the load-bearing decision. vitest-evals writes task.meta.eval from
applyAutomaticJudges (dist/index.mjs:1393) and from appendJudgeScore, the explicit
toSatisfyJudge path (:1447). Both are reachable only from a result run(...) handed back;
clearRecordedTaskMeta (:1229) blanks the metadata first; the catch path writes only
meta.harness before rethrowing. So a throwing harness publishes no score, whereas an expect()
in the test body runs after both writers: at :1393 the write is unconditional and the
threshold assert fires afterwards, so the number is published first and the failure raised
second. Choosing between automatic and explicit judges is not a fix: the surface is any judge
that scores on a degenerate run.

Proven on the emitted JSON both ways, with a control exercising the path the case must avoid:
  healthy     passed  meta.eval PRESENT avg=1  meta.harness present
  degenerate  failed  meta.eval ABSENT         meta.harness present
The control is not decoration: with the precondition throwing in both fixtures, "does not
publish" and "never ran" predict the same observation and the test cannot discriminate.

RUNNER: one vitest config scoped to tests/evals/**/*.eval.ts, disjoint from `bun test` by FILE
EXTENSION rather than a second bunfig ignore pattern, so the four existing bun eval suites
stay put and ladder.ts's TEST_FILE regex cannot see these files. It must run under
`bun --bun`: the spine opens the agent store through bun:sqlite, and node-hosted vitest
collects ZERO tests, which would read as a clean tier. Replay is off and .vitest-evals/
gitignored: recordings capture tool INPUT verbatim, which for an agent harness is where a
bearer lives. Corpus is additive: seed.jsonl untouched, its no-tool cases filtered by tag,
because a task that hands over no environment cannot exercise any mechanism.

Also fixes a defect the panel shipped with: tool_outcomes counted only the transport `error`
flag, so a command that ran and exited non-zero, an ordinary successful result whose text
begins `Error (exit N)`, scored as clean. Adds isFailingResultText beside formatExecResult,
the renderer that writes that prefix, as the one definition. The same confusion graded a
command exiting 3 as `accepted` at quality 0.70 in the evolution reward: the worst call in the
turn contributing the best number.

84/84 across test-utils and the artifact contract; `bun run check` exit 0.

THE FIRST LIVE RECORDS. 36 episodes against @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 through
the deployed worker proxy, the first live-model behavioural measurement this project has. The
two records here are the paired flash runs; both are ADMISSIBLE.

  flash-a  14 graded turns, 126 tool calls, 2,623,902 in / 59,796 out
  flash-b  13 graded turns, 113 tool calls, 2,199,758 in / 50,427 out
  delegation_conversion  0.154 / 0.167     steering_conversion 0.143 / 0.167
  edit_landing           1.000 / 1.000     tool_outcomes       0.817 / 0.903
  craft_reuse, completion_honesty, spill_retrieval: NO eligible opportunity

That last line is the point of the denominator discipline. Three mechanisms were never
exercised by this corpus, and they report absent rather than zero: "could not" is a fact about
the tasks, "did not" is a fact about the agent, and collapsing them is how a corpus that never
reached a mechanism comes to read as an agent that never uses it.

The comparison refuses to overclaim. Every scorer whose paired tasks differed fewer than 6
times leads with UNDECIDABLE and prints the floor from the DIFFERING count, not the task
count. tool_outcomes moved +5.9pp with CI [+2.0pp, +9.9pp] and is still UNDECIDABLE: only 4 of
6 paired tasks differed, so the best two-sided p reachable is 0.1250. That is the exact error
CL-Bench made when it read a -20pp gain whose true floor was p=0.5 over 2 differing pairs.
recovery_durability is reported as a change in what the corpus REACHED rather than a
behavioural delta, because it had an opportunity in one run and none in the other.

Both records carry the arm state (evolution ON, settle none, 8 tools), the model id, the seed,
the repeat count and the git sha, and both are flagged DIRTY, honestly, since the tree carried
untracked scratch when they were produced. A record that cannot say what produced it is not
comparable.

* feat(orgs): OrganizationInvitation + OrganizationMember entities

The `OrganizationMember` / `OrganizationInvitation` pair that
docs/specs/features/tenants-and-organizations/spec.md §7 defers to v1.1.
Entities and registration only — no behaviour yet.

🛑 organization_members is the ROSTER, not the authorization check. Access
stays `user.tenantId === organization.tenantId` via
OrganizationMembershipService.ensureMember, unchanged. Five independent read
paths depend on that equality (ensureMember, OrganizationService.listForUser,
ScopeOwnershipGuard, TeamsService.listOrgUsers, TeamsService.addMember), and
rewriting them is a far larger change than adding invitations. The table
answers what tenant-equality cannot: who invited this person, when they
joined, and for which Organization — and it is the seam a future per-Org
permission model tightens without a second migration.

Two deliberate tightenings versus the WorkInvitation template:

  - `email` is NOT NULL. WorkInvitation.email is nullable because a Work
    invite can be a bare link handed over out of band. An Org invite exists
    to reach someone with no account, and the mail path silently no-ops on a
    null recipient — nullable would make "invited someone unreachable"
    representable.
  - A partial unique index on (organizationId, emailNormalized) WHERE
    status = 'pending'. Without it, clicking invite twice mints two
    independently redeemable tokens for one mailbox and revoking the visible
    one leaves the other live. Partial, so re-inviting after a revoke or an
    expiry stays legal.

`emailNormalized` is stored rather than derived because the uniqueness index
and the accept-time comparison must agree on one canonical form; computing it
in two places is how "already invited" and "not invited" end up both true.

ORGANIZATION_MEMBER_ROLES has exactly one value on purpose.
OrganizationMembershipService.ensureAdmin is currently
`return this.ensureMember(...)` and its docblock forbids adding a role check
without a product decision, so shipping an `admin` option would put a control
in the UI that grants nothing.

Verified: 54/54 in the database config + module specs. Control: removing
OrganizationMember from _entity-names.ts fails
"entity-names inventory drift (EW-638)", so the registration is genuinely
locked, not just present. tsc adds zero errors (3 before and after on a clean
tree — all the pre-existing missing @modelcontextprotocol/sdk install).

* feat(orgs): migration for organization_invitations + organization_members

Additive only: two new tables, no column dropped, no data touched.

🛑 Why this file gets more scrutiny than most: DATABASE_AUTOMIGRATE (TypeORM
`synchronize`) is TRUE in dev and stage and FALSE in prod — verified on the
live Secrets of ever-works-app-{dev,stage,prod}. In dev and stage,
`synchronize` builds these tables from the entities whether or not this
migration works, so a defect here is invisible in both lower environments and
first appears as a crash-looping prod pod. A green dev rollout is not
evidence for this file.

So it was verified on BOTH engines:

  - Committed spec (better-sqlite3, what CI and e2e run): 4/4 — creation,
    idempotent re-run, down(), and the partial-index behaviour.
  - A throwaway Postgres 16 in Docker, the engine prod actually uses:
    up, up-again, indexes, behaviour, and down all confirmed. The partial
    index is genuinely partial there —
    WHERE ((status)::text = 'pending'::text) — a duplicate PENDING invite is
    rejected, a re-invite after a revoke is accepted, and `id` really does
    default to uuid_generate_v4().

The SQLite pass caught a real defect the Postgres run never would have:
`default: 'now()'` is Postgres-only, and demo/e2e are SQLite. It failed at
INSERT, not at DDL, so the three schema-shape tests passed while the default
was broken. Now CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, matching the house convention in
CreateTeamsTables and AddPluginUsageEvents.

its pending invitations and roster with it; SET NULL on acceptedByUserId and
on organization_members.invitationId, so deleting a user or pruning an
invitation never erases the record that someone joined.

* feat(orgs): invitation token lifecycle — service + repositories

Clones WorkInvitationService's security properties so the two adjacent
features cannot drift: randomBytes(32) token, sha256 stored and the raw value
returned exactly once, lookup by hash so the token never appears in a query,
and a conditional UPDATE for accept so two people redeeming one token resolve
with exactly one winner.

🛑 One deliberate divergence: the ORG token is EMAIL-BOUND, the Work token is
a bearer credential. Accepting an org invitation writes users.tenantId, which
grants access to every Organization in that Tenant — a much larger blast
radius than joining one Work, so a forwarded email must not be enough.
findConsumable() takes the redeemer's address and refuses a mismatch; it stays
optional only for the signed-out preview page, which grants nothing.

normaliseEmail case-folds and trims but deliberately does NOT strip dots or
plus tags. Those are Gmail conventions, not SMTP ones — applying them would
make a.b@corp.com and ab@corp.com the same person on a domain where they are
two different employees.

The 409 for a duplicate invite comes from the partial unique index, not from a
prior SELECT: two clicks a millisecond apart both pass a read-then-write check
and mint two live tokens for one mailbox.

Verified: 19/19. Control: storing the raw token and dropping the email binding
fails exactly 3 tests — "persists ONLY the hash", "refuses a redeemer whose
address is not the invited one", and the prefix case — and nothing else.

The spec also documents a trap it hit: isUniqueConstraintError reads
err.driverError.code, so a test that sets .code on the QueryFailedError
wrapper sails straight past the guard and proves nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(orgs): joinTenant — the single audited writer of a foreign users.tenantId

Accepting an org invitation has to put the invitee in the Organization's
Tenant, because that equality IS the authorization check. This is the third
writer of users.tenantId in the codebase and the only one that ever points a
user at a Tenant somebody else owns, so it lives beside ensureTenant to keep
every write to that column in one audited file.

🛑 It will NOT move a user between Tenants. Hard refusal, not best-effort,
for four independent reasons:

  1. Every row the user already created is stamped with their OLD tenantId by
     ScopeStampingSubscriber and by createOrganization. Repointing orphans all
     of it — the rows keep the old tenant, so their whole history silently
     vanishes from the scope they can now see. Data loss without a DELETE.
  2. tenants.ownerUserId is UNIQUE, so an owner cannot cleanly stop owning;
     repointing leaves an owner-linked, member-less orphan Tenant.
  3. listForUser returns every Org of user.tenantId, so repointing instantly
     hides all of their own Organizations from them.
  4. The FK on users.tenantId is ON DELETE SET NULL — there is no
     database-level protection. The guard must be in code, and tested.

It also deliberately does NOT run createOrganization's TIER_A/TIER_B
backfill: dragging an invitee's pre-existing private rows into the inviter's
Tenant would expose their history tenant-wide. Their own Works stay reachable
because WorkRepository filters on userId, never tenantId.

Verified: 11/11 (5 pre-existing + 6 new). Control: replacing the refusal with
a silent repoint fails exactly one test — "🛑 REFUSES to move a user who
already belongs to a different Tenant" — and nothing else.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(orgs): invitation issuance API + the accept/remove flow service

Routes on the existing api/organizations/:orgId family, so they inherit
AuthSessionGuard + OrganizationOwnershipGuard unchanged: caller must already
be a member, and failures are 404 not 403, so none of this can be used to
probe which Organization ids exist.

🛑 The token is never returned by any route, not even to the issuer — it
exists only inside the email. A token echoed into an API response lands in
browser history, proxy logs and screenshots, and it grants tenant-wide
access; the one-way sha256 in the database is pointless if the plaintext
comes back over HTTP.

POST invitations is throttled at 10/min rather than the 30/min the other
org writes use, because it makes the server send mail to an arbitrary
address — a spam vector as well as a write.

accept() orders its steps deliberately: validate + email-bind, THEN
joinTenant (which may refuse), THEN the conditional UPDATE, THEN the roster
row. joinTenant runs before the invitation is burned so that a refusal
leaves the invitation still redeemable — burning it on failure would strand
the invitee with no way back.

removeMember closes the one-way door the owner asked about: it deletes the
roster row and, ONLY when that was the person's last membership in the
Tenant, clears users.tenantId back to NULL so ensureTenant can lazily give
them their own Tenant again. It refuses to remove the Tenant owner, who is a
member by construction and whose removal would orphan every Organization in
the Tenant. Nothing else is deleted.

Verified: 3/3 wiring tests. Control: swapping two constructor parameters —
which tsc accepts, because Nest injects POSITIONALLY — fails "asks for
exactly the collaborators it needs, in order". That is the class of bug this
spec exists for: it compiles, then crash-loops every pod at boot, which tsc
cannot see.

Also caught while writing this: OrganizationRepository has no
isTenantOwnedBy — I had invented it. Ownership now reads
TenantRepository.findById().ownerUserId, which is UNIQUE, so one read settles
it.

* feat(orgs): email the invitation — template, send method, and wiring

An invite that reaches nobody is not an invite, so this is the half that
makes the feature real: a new organization-invitation.hbs, a
MailService.sendOrganizationInvitation, and the call from the flow service
with the accept URL built from config.webAppUrl().

🛑 The acceptUrl carries the RAW token, and that email body is the only
place it ever appears — the row holds sha256(token) and no API response
returns it. So the send method never interpolates `data` into a log line;
the catch logs the recipient and the error only.

The email states the recipient address explicitly. The token is email-bound,
so redeeming it while signed in as a different account 403s, and the email is
the only place that can explain that before it happens rather than after.

Verified against real infrastructure rather than assumed:
  - Mail is genuinely configured in all three environments — MAILER_PROVIDER
    is `resend` with SMTP_HOST and EMAIL_FROM set on dev, stage AND prod.
  - The .hbs files really do ship inside the running prod image: 10 present
    at /app/dist/templates, negative control 0. The historical ENOENT defect
    that made signup-confirmation unreachable is gone.
  - `nest build -b swc` copies the new template into dist (11/11) via the
    existing `templates/**/*` asset glob, and reports 0 TSC issues.

Verified: 75/75 across the mail and wiring suites. Control: renaming
{{acceptUrl}} to {{acceptURL}} — a one-character typo — fails "renders the
organization invitation with a working accept link". That is the failure
mode worth guarding: Handlebars renders an unknown variable as an EMPTY
STRING rather than throwing, so the typo would have shipped an email with a
dead Accept button and nothing anywhere would have reported a problem.

Two lock lists also had to be updated, both doing their job by noticing a new
template: KNOWN_EMAIL_TEMPLATES (two-way checked against the directory) and

* feat(orgs): public preview + authenticated accept for org invitations

The half that makes a BRAND-NEW person work. Split into a @Public() preview
and an authenticated accept, mirroring ClaimController: the invitee clicks
the link with no account, sees "you have been invited to Acme", registers or
signs in, and only then does accept run.

Lives in OnboardingModule rather than on the api/organizations/:orgId family
because those routes sit behind OrganizationOwnershipGuard — which requires
exactly the membership the invitee does not have yet. That is not a detail:
putting the accept route there would make it unreachable by every person it
exists to serve.

🛑 The preview MASKS the invited address (a***@example.com). It is public to
anyone holding the token, so returning it in full would turn a forwarded or
leaked link into an address disclosure. Masked is still enough for the real
job — telling the recipient which of their accounts to sign in as, which they
need because the token is email-bound. This is a deliberate divergence from
the Work claim preview, which returns its address in full; the divergence is
in the safer direction.

The preview deliberately calls findConsumable WITHOUT a redeemer address:
there is no signed-in user yet, and it grants nothing. Passing one would 403
exactly the people the route is for.

The accept DTO pins the token at exactly 64 characters (randomBytes(32) as
hex), so a truncated or padded value is rejected before it reaches a database
lookup and the public surface cannot be used as an oracle for token length.
Both routes throttle at 10/min per IP, matching the claim preview.

Verified: 138/138 across the onboarding, organizations and mail suites; the
full API compiles with TSC reporting 0 issues. Control: returning
invitation.email instead of maskEmail(...) fails exactly the two masking
tests and nothing else.

Also exported OrganizationInvitationFlowService and
OrganizationInvitationService from OrganizationsModule — without that the
accept route resolves at compile time and dies at BOOT, which is the failure
class the wiring spec exists to catch.

* feat(orgs): make /org-invite/:token reachable while signed out

The invitation landing page is hit by a BRAND-NEW person straight from an
email, with no account and no session — which is the entire point of the
feature. proxy.ts bounces an unauthenticated request for a non-public route
to /login, CLEARS the auth cookie, and preserves no token. So a missing entry
here would not merely redirect: it would destroy the invitation the visitor
was sent, showing them a login screen with nothing logged anywhere.

Three sibling routes already exist for exactly this reason and each carries a
comment saying so — the magic-link landing page, resend-verification, and the
onboarding hand-off. This is the fourth, and the only one reached by someone
who has no account at all.

Adds a public-routes spec, which the repo had none of. Verified 6/6, with a
CONTROL asserting /dashboard, /settings and /teams/:id are NOT public — so an
always-true matcher could not make the rest pass vacuously. Second control:
deleting ROUTES.ORG_INVITE from PUBLIC_ROUTES (the precise mistake) fails
exactly 3 tests.

Also covers two things that would each break every live invitation at once:
the route must match any token shape rather than today's 64 hex characters,
and it must NOT open the whole /org-invite namespace, since `:token` is a
single segment.

* feat(orgs): the invitation landing page — where a newcomer actually arrives

Completes the round trip: /org-invite/[token] renders signed-out, previews
the invitation, and offers accept / sign in / create an account. Modelled on
the sibling /claim/[token] page, with two deliberate differences, both because
this route serves OUTSIDERS rather than existing users.

First, it names the reason a link failed instead of showing one generic
error. A visitor with no account cannot debug anything, and "expired",
"cancelled" and "wrong account" need opposite responses — only one of them is
worth emailing anyone about.

Second, both auth links STASH the invitation in redirect_url before
navigating. Without that a brand-new person registers, lands on the
dashboard, and their invitation is silently spent — the exact failure the
whole signed-out path exists to prevent. The stored value is a relative path,
so it cannot become an open redirect (and getRedirectUrl validates it again
on the way out).

🔑 Two specs, and the second exists because a control proved the first was
not enough: OrgInviteForm.unit.spec.tsx MOCKS the actions module, so deleting
setRedirectCookie from the real action left it fully green — it can prove the
component calls the action and nothing about what the action does. The new
org-invite.unit.spec.ts covers the action itself, and the same control now
fails exactly 3 of its tests.

* fix(orgs): boot crash + two ways an invitee could gain unrevocable access

Three defects found by an adversarial review of this branch, all confirmed by
reading the code rather than taken on trust.

1. CRITICAL — the API would have crash-looped at boot.
   OrganizationsModule declares a controller using @UseGuards(AuthSessionGuard)
   but never imported AuthModule. AuthModule is NOT @Global and
   AuthSessionGuard uses constructor injection, so Nest cannot resolve it —
   "Nest can't resolve dependencies", every pod, on startup. TeamsModule
   imports it for exactly this reason. tsc cannot see this, and my own
   module-wiring spec missed it because it only checked the flow service's
   paramtypes, not the controller's guards.

2. HIGH — accept() granted access before claiming the token.
   joinTenant COMMITS users.tenantId, and only then did tryAccept run the
   conditional UPDATE. If a revoke landed in that window the claim failed, the
   code threw, and nothing rolled back: the invitee kept TENANT-WIDE access
   with no roster row — invisible in the members list (which reads the roster)
   and not removable via removeMember (which needs one). A revoked invitation
   still granted access.

   My docblock argued for that ordering. It was wrong: it reasoned only about
   the refusal case and never considered a successful join followed by a lost
   claim. Whatever gate authorizes access has to be the atomic one, so the
   claim now runs FIRST and the grant only happens if it wins.

   The double-click path is also now precise — it checks
   acceptedByUserId === userId instead of inferring "it was me" from a failed
   re-read, which previously also matched a REVOKED invitation and reported
   success for it.

3. HIGH — joinTenant's check-then-update was a TOCTOU.
   Two invitations accepted at the same instant both observed
   `tenantId IS NULL` and both wrote, homing the user in whichever tenant
   committed last while BOTH invitations were marked accepted. Now a
   conditional UPDATE (UserRepository.claimTenantIfUnassigned,
   WHERE "tenantId" IS NULL) lets the database arbitrate; losing to the SAME
   tenant is idempotent success, losing to a different one is the existing
   refusal.

Two review findings with one root cause: the members endpoint returned bare
userIds, so the UI had nothing to render and no way to tell which row was the
person looking at it.

  - The roster rendered `m.userId`, i.e. a raw UUID. Unusable for the one

  - The "is this me?" check compared against a `currentUserId` prop that the

listMembers now resolves each row to a person and returns `username`, `email`
and a SERVER-COMPUTED `isSelf`. Computing isSelf server-side is the point: the
caller's identity is already known there, and a client that has to be told its
own id separately is a client that will one day forget to — which is exactly
what happened. The `currentUserId` prop is gone rather than left as a trap.

same person reads the same way in both places. userId survives only as the

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(orgs): keep the invitation token out of URLs, logs and Sentry

The public preview took the token as a query parameter, so the full 64-hex
tenant-granting credential appeared in the request URL — and this repo
persists URLs in two places:

  - logging.interceptor.ts logs `Incoming Request: ${method} ${originalUrl}`,
    which its own comment notes is forwarded on as $log events.
  - Sentry attaches `event.request.url`, query string included, to transaction
    events. Its scrubber only matches pathnames under `/auth`, so
    /api/org-invite/preview was not covered.

That defeated the design outright. The database stores only sha256(token)
precisely so the plaintext exists in exactly one place — the email body — and
a token in a URL undoes that with no other change required.

Preview is now a POST carrying the token in the body, which neither of those
two paths captures. A POST for a read is deliberate, and the same shape token
introspection endpoints use.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(orgs): write the roster row BEFORE granting access, not after

accept() makes three separate commits with no enclosing transaction —
joinTenant writes through a different repository — so some partial state is
unavoidable. The real choice is which partial state to prefer, and the
deciding property is VISIBILITY.

Previously the grant came first, so a failing roster write left the person
with TENANT-WIDE ACCESS and no roster row: invisible in the members list, and
removeMember refuses with `not_a_member` because there is no row to delete.
That is precisely the unrevocable state this method was already fixed once to
avoid, reachable through a second door.

Reversed, the worst case is a roster row with no access: the person shows up
in the members list, an admin can see and remove them, and re-accepting
repairs it. Harmless and self-announcing.

recordMembership is idempotent, so writing it first costs nothing on the
happy path. The duplicate call after the grant is gone.

* fix(orgs): an expired invitation no longer blocks re-inviting that person forever

The partial unique index is WHERE status = 'pending', and NOTHING moves a row
from pending to expired on a timer — expireBefore exists but nobody calls it.
So an invitation that aged out still occupies the slot: re-inviting the same
address fails with `invitation_already_pending`, telling the admin there is a
live invitation when the token behind it is dead.

That was permanent. The pending-invitations list would show it, but revoking
is the only lever and revoking an invitation you were told is pending — in
order to send the same person the same invitation — is not a step anyone
would guess at.

issue() now retires the aged-out row for that one (organization, email) pair
before inserting. Scoped rather than a table sweep, so issuing an invitation
stays a bounded write, and best-effort (.catch) so a sweep failure cannot
block a legitimate invite — the index still protects correctness either way.

also asserts the sweep happens BEFORE the insert — the other order would be
rejected by the index first and prove nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(orgs): a failed invitation email no longer strands an unusable pending row

The invitation row commits before the mail call, and the raw token exists in
exactly one place — that email. So a send failure left a row whose token
reached NOBODY and which cannot be recovered, because the database holds only
sha256.

Left pending, that row is worse than useless: the partial unique index on
(organizationId, emailNormalized) WHERE status='pending' BLOCKS re-inviting
the address, and there is no resend endpoint. The admin is told an invitation
is pending for a token that does not exist anywhere, and the obvious
response — send it again — is refused.

invite() now revokes the invitation when the send fails, releasing the address
immediately so retrying works, and rethrows so the caller reports the failure
instead of claiming an invite went out. The revoke is best-effort: a secondary
failure while tidying up must not replace the mail error, which is the one the
admin actually needs to see.

New spec, 5/5, with two controls: a successful send must NOT revoke (or the
main assertion would pass for the wrong reason), and removing the revoke call
fails exactly the one test — verified by counting occurrences before and after
arming, 1 -> 0, because a control that quietly fails to arm looks identical to
a passing one.

Verified: 12 suites / 71 tests across organizations + onboarding, `nest build`
TSC 0 issues.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(conversations): PATCH {"title": null} no longer nulls the title

`@IsOptional()` skips every other validator when the value is `null` as well
as when it is `undefined` — class-validator's condition is literally
`value !== null && value !== undefined`. So `PATCH {"title": null}` sailed
past `@IsString`, then satisfied the handler's `body.title !== undefined`
guard (because `null !== undefined`) and WROTE NULL over the user's title.

It was a hard 400 before the field became optional in #2103, and the DTO's own
docblock still claimed non-string payloads were rejected. They were not.

Replaced with `@ValidateIf(o => o.title !== undefined)`, which restores the
intent exactly: absent is fine, present-but-not-a-string is a 400. Same
treatment for `model`, where a null slipped through to `updateModel` and
happened to coincide with the clear-the-pin branch — harmless, but it made the
documented contract false.

The E2E suite could not have caught this: those specs probe the empty body
`{}`, never an explicit null.

Verified: new DTO spec 11/11, whole ai-conversation suite 106/106, `nest build`
TSC 0 issues. Controls: four "must stay valid" cases (empty body, title-only,
model-only, model:'' clear-the-pin) so a DTO that rejected everything could not
pass by accident; and reverting to @IsOptional() fails exactly the three null
tests — confirmed by counting the ValidateIf occurrences before and after
arming, 2 -> 0.

Found while investigating why stage E2E was red. Unrelated to that red, and
unrelated to the Teams fix being promoted.

def has_perm(self, perm, obj=None):
        """
        Return True if the user has the specified permission. Query all
        available auth backends, but return immediately if any backend returns
        True. Thus, a user who has permission from a single auth backend is
        assumed to have permission in general. If an object is provided, check
        permissions for that object.
        """
        # Active superusers have all permissions.
        if self.is_active and self.is_superuser:

        # Otherwise we need to check the backends.

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: posture-staleness-alert
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: posture-staleness-alert
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: posture-staleness-alert
    namespace: observability

# What the posture-staleness-alert CronJob may read.
#
# Read-only, and ONLY the stored configuration-scan objects. The check has to see
# scans in every scanned namespace to find the newest one, so it is cluster-scoped
# by necessity — but it is list-only on a single resource type, which is the least
# privilege that satisfies that.
#
# It deliberately does NOT grant the summary kinds. Those carry a zero-valued
# creationTimestamp, so they cannot answer a freshness question and reading them
# would widen the grant for no signal.
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: posture-staleness-alert
rules:
  - apiGroups:
      - spdx.softwarecomposition.kubescape.io
    resources:
      - workloadconfigurationscans
    verbs:
      - list

# Alerts when Kubescape's stored configuration-scan data stops moving.
#
# WHY THIS EXISTS
#
# A broken posture scanner and a compliant cluster read IDENTICALLY. When the
# scan aborts it persists nothing, so every consumer sees "no new findings" —
# which is exactly what a clean cluster looks like. Nothing anywhere treats that
# as a failure.
#
# That is not hypothetical. Measured on prod 2026-08-19 while picking up #3024:
# the newest stored `workloadconfigurationscan` was 2026-06-27 — posture had been
# frozen for FIFTY-THREE DAYS and no signal existed on any surface. The scheduler
# CronJob kept reporting `lastSuccessfulTime` daily (it only POSTs the scan
# request; it does not observe the outcome) and the CI posture gate stayed green
# (it scans manifests, not the cluster). The control that rules out the storage
# layer: `applicationprofiles` and `vulnerabilitymanifestsummaries`, served by the
# same aggregated API, were fresh to the same day.
#
# This check keys on DATA AGE rather than on any particular failure. #2933's
# original cause (offline mode starving the policy-artifact fetch) had already
# been fixed and the scan was failing a THIRD way by the time this was written —
# so a rule that watched for a known error string would have gone quiet exactly
# when it mattered. Age covers every abort cause, including the next one.
#
# WHY IT PAGINATES — this is load-bearing, not defensive habit
#
# The aggregated storage API returns a `continue` token: a single unpaginated GET
# returns only the first page. Measured, the collection is 1542 objects over 4
# pages of 500. Taking the newest timestamp from page 1 alone would report an
# arbitrary subset's maximum as though it were the collection's — silently, and
# in either direction. The loop below follows `continue` to exhaustion and fails
# loudly if it does not terminate, rather than reporting a partial answer.
#
# WHY ZERO OBJECTS ALERTS RATHER THAN PASSES
#
# An empty collection is the silent zero this check exists to catch, so it is
# treated as a failure signal — never as "nothing to report". Same reasoning as
# the non-200 and response-shape guards.
#
# Lives in the observability namespace to reuse the allow-coroot
# CiliumNetworkPolicy (endpointSelector: {}), which already permits
# kube-apiserver, hooks.slack.com:443 and DNS egress — the same reason
# cron-job-cnpg-degraded-alert.yaml sits here despite bein

* Per-category delivery explanation on product pages + Discord

Answers the #1 pre-purchase question ('how do I get it?') right on each
product, and mirrors it in Discord.

- src/lib/deliveryInfo.js: bilingual (EN/NL) delivery info per category —

button that applies a ~18% markup with a €2 minimum profit, rounded to a
clean .99 — so €140 cost → €165.99, €10 → €11.99. Tune MARKUP/FLOOR in one
place. Existing margin readout stays.

* delivery: drop the Roblox-group join step from Robux (group is only for giveaways)

Robux delivery no longer mentions joining a Roblox group — the group is used
for giveaways, not delivery. Steps are now: enable 2FA → send your username →

* Forge Coins + Forge Shop, and 'as fast as possible' delivery label

  no cached number that can drift). Earn 1 coin per €10 of paid spend,

- Migration 012_forge_coins.
- Product page: replaced the 'Estimated delivery ~Xs' line with a simple

Verified on real Postgres: earn/idempotency/redeem/overspend all pass; build green.

* Mystery boxes — a real paid 'giveaway' (buy → roll a weighted prize → store credit)

- Migration 013: mystery_box_rewards (weighted prize pool) + mystery_pulls
  (what each buyer won). A mystery box is a product with kind='mystery'.
- mysteryBoxService: weighted roll per unit on payment, pays out as store
  credit via the wallet (tagged = idempotent, no double-pay on retries),
  records the pull + notifies the buyer.
- Hooked into order payment_received.
- Admin: 'Mystery box' toggle + a reward-pool editor (label / odds / € credit)
  in the product modal (GET+PUT /admin/products/:id/mystery).
- Product page: 'What's inside' panel showing every prize + REAL odds.
- Account order page: a celebratory reveal of what you won + credit added.
- Public GET /products/:id/mystery (pool+odds), account GET /orders/:id/mystery.

Verified on real Postgres: roll/credit/record + idempotent re-settle (6/6);
build green. Note: bundles already support any product mix (PS+Xbox, Apex+
Valorant) — create them in Admin → Monetization.

* i18n: Dutch labels for the mystery-box 'What's inside' panel

* Mystery boxes: bulk-luck ('more = better prizes') + a risk-free reroll (1x/box)

- Odds now scale with how many boxes are opened in one order: +8% luck per
  extra box (capped 2x), weighted toward the higher-value prizes — buy more,
  win better. Verified over a large sample (avg prize rises with quantity).
- One reroll per box (migration 014 stamps rerolled_at, claimed atomically so
  it can't be used twice): rolls a fresh prize and the buyer KEEPS the higher
  one — risk-free. POST /account/orders/:id/mystery/:pullId/reroll + a Reroll
  button on the order reveal.

Verified on real Postgres: reroll keeps-the-better + second reroll blocked; build green.

- Migration 015 + dropService: staff schedule drops (title, category, note,

- Public GET /api/drops (upcoming); admin GET/POST/DELETE /api/admin/drops.

- Admin: a 'Drops' tab in Monetization to schedule/remove drops.
- New drops announce to Discord (best-effort).

Verified on real Postgres (5/5: create/upcoming filter/list/delete); build green.

* Price history chart on product pages

- Migration 016 + price_history: a snapshot on product create and on every

- Public GET /api/products/:id/price-history.
